stages.name: How it performs
stages.html:
"The two queries scale differently."

Query Cost per room with n bookings
Pairs self-join up to n² comparisons; the output itself can be n²
Sweep sort 2n points, one pass
Design Effect
Index on (room_id, start_ts) the join seeks by room and the first inequality
A range type with a GiST index (PostgreSQL) overlap lookups become index searches

What breaks at scale: "check then insert" under concurrency. Two requests both see the room free. The guard has to be a constraint or a lock on the room.

Fix layer: the query for detection, a constraint for prevention.

followUps.question: "Check whether either end of one falls inside the other."
followUps.html:
That misses containment from one side.

Case "An end of a is inside b" Two inequalities
a = 09:00–11:00, b = 10:30–10:45 neither end of a is inside b

followUps.question: 🧪 Booking 2 ends at 12:00 and booking 5 starts at 12:00. With the half-open test, do they overlap?
followUps.html:
No.

a = booking 2 (10:00–12:00), b = booking 5 (12:00–12:30)
a.start < b.end   → 10:00 < 12:30   true
b.start < a.end   → 12:00 < 12:00   false      ← run on the sample: no (2,5) pair

followUps.question: Why order the sweep by t, then d?
followUps.html:
So an end is applied before a start at the same instant.

At 12:00: one ends, one starts Running count
−1 first, then +1 1 → 0 → 1
+1 first, then −1 1 → 2 → 1

followUps.question: How do you check a new booking before inserting it?
followUps.html:
One existence test with the same two inequalities.

  • NOT EXISTS (… WHERE room_id = :room AND start_ts < :new_end AND :new_start < end_ts)
  • And a constraint or a lock, because the check alone races.

followUps.question: Two users book the same slot at the same moment. What stops a double booking?
followUps.html:
The database, not the check.

Guard How
An exclusion constraint (PostgreSQL) the second insert fails
Lock the room row (SELECT … FOR UPDATE), check, insert serialises bookings per room
Serializable isolation one transaction aborts and retries

dontSay: "I'd list the overlap cases." — two inequalities cover all of them.
"BETWEEN." — it's closed at both ends.
"A loop over every minute." — sweep the endpoints.
"We check availability before inserting." — two requests race.

databases-q15.testing: cohort analysis: fixing each user's first day, then counting who came back, without losing the users who didn't.
databases-q15.trap: an inner join to the day-after logins, which removes the non-returners from the denominator.
databases-q15.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Read the tables "One table, logins, with a user and a date. I'll take a user's first login as their signup day. Day-one retention is: of the users who started on a given day, what share logged in again on the very next day."
2 · Name the pattern "This is a cohort query. Step one, find each user's first day. Step two, for each user, check whether a login exists on first day plus one. Step three, group by the first day."
3 · Write it "A CTE gets the minimum login date per user. Then I left join logins on the same user and the date equal to the first day plus one, group by the first day, and count distinct users on each side."
4 · Trace it on data "Both users start on the first of March. User one is back on the second; user two's next login is the third. So the cohort has two users, one returned, fifty percent."
5 · Variants and traps "It has to be a left join. With an inner join only the returners survive, and retention reads as a hundred percent. And I count distinct users, because someone can log in twice on day one."
6 · How it performs "An index on user and date makes the day-after check a seek."
Close "First day per user, left join to the day after, distinct counts."

stages.name: Read the tables
stages.html:
"Two definitions to agree before writing."

logins(user_id, login_date)
user_id logins first day back on first day + 1?
1 03-01, 03-02, 03-03, 03-07, 03-08 03-01 03-02
2 03-01, 03-03, 03-08 03-01
Definition Choice here
Cohort users grouped by their first login date
Day-1 retained a login exactly one calendar day later (not "within a day", not "ever again")

Output: cohort, users, back_day_1, pct.

stages.name: Name the pattern
stages.claim: first event, then a look-ahead join
stages.html:
"Pin each user to a start date; everything else is measured from it."

Pattern:MIN(date) per userleft join activity on date = first + Ngroup by the first datereturners / cohort size
Clue in the question Pattern
"retention", "cohort", "came back after N days" first event + offset join
"churned" the same, counting the rows with no match

stages.name: Write it
stages.claim: a cohort CTE and a LEFT JOIN
stages.html:
"The left side is the denominator; the right side is the numerator." Run on SQLite 3.51.

WITH first AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(login_date) AS d0
  FROM logins GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT f.d0 AS cohort,
       COUNT(DISTINCT f.user_id) AS users,
       COUNT(DISTINCT l.user_id) AS back_day_1,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT l.user_id)
             / COUNT(DISTINCT f.user_id), 1) AS pct
FROM first f
LEFT JOIN logins l
  ON l.user_id = f.user_id
 AND l.login_date = date(f.d0, '+1 day')
GROUP BY f.d0;
cohort users back_day_1 pct
2026-03-01 2 1 50.0

stages.name: Trace it on data
stages.html:
"What the left join produces before grouping."

f.user_id f.d0 looks for a login on l.user_id counted in users counted in back_day_1
1 03-01 03-02 1
2 03-01 03-02 NULL —

COUNT(DISTINCT l.user_id) ignores the NULL, so user 2 is in the denominator and not in the numerator: 1 / 2 = 50%.

stages.name: Variants and traps
stages.html:
"The same query with JOIN in place of LEFT JOIN." Run on the sample.

Join users back_day_1 Retention
LEFT JOIN 2 1 50%
JOIN 1 1 100%
Trap What happens
Inner join non-returners vanish from the cohort
The day-after test in WHERE turns the left join back into an inner join
COUNT(*) two logins on day 1 count the user twice
Integer division 1 / 2 = 0
The most recent cohort day + 1 hasn't happened yet: exclude it, or it reads as 0%
Variant asked next Change
Day-7 date(f.d0, '+7 day')
Day 1, 7 and 30 as columns a join on login_date > d0, then COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN offset = 1 THEN user_id END) per column
Weekly cohorts truncate d0 to the week
An EXISTS form (run on the sample: 2 users, 1 back) SUM(EXISTS (…)) per cohort; no duplicates to worry about
PostgreSQL f.d0 + 1 or + INTERVAL '1 day'

stages.name: How it performs
stages.html:
"The cohort CTE scans; the look-ahead seeks."

Design Effect
Index on (user_id, login_date) MIN per user is the first entry; the day-after check is a seek
One row per user per day (a daily activity table) removes duplicates and shrinks the scan
A stored signup_date on the user the cohort step disappears

What breaks at scale: recomputing every cohort over all history. A cohort's day-1 number never changes once day 1 has passed, so it's computed once and stored.

Fix layer: the query for correctness, a retention table for cost.

followUps.question: "Join logins to itself on user and date + 1, then count."
followUps.html:
An inner self-join keeps only the people who came back.

Denominator
Inner join returners only → 100%
Left join from the cohort everyone who started

followUps.question: 🧪 On the sample, what does the inner-join version report for the 03-01 cohort?
followUps.html:
1 user, 1 back: 100%.

user 2 has no login on 03-02 → no joined row → gone from the cohort
users = 1, back = 1                               ← run on the sample

followUps.question: Why is "first login" a weak definition of signup?
followUps.html:
It depends on the data you happen to have.

  • A log that starts mid-history makes old users look new on its first day.
  • Better: a signup_date column on the user.

followUps.question: "Day 1" in whose time zone?
followUps.html:
It has to be chosen, and it changes the number.

Choice Effect
UTC dates a user at 23:30 local can be "back the next day" 40 minutes later
The user's local date matches behaviour; needs the zone stored
A rolling 24–48 hours after signup no calendar edge; a different metric

followUps.question: Retention dropped five points this week. How do you investigate?
followUps.html:
Check the measurement, then segment.

Step Question
Is the cohort complete? has day + 1 fully passed, and did all events load?
Did the definition change? a new login event, a tracking gap
Which segment moved? by platform, channel, country, app version

dontSay: "Inner join to the next day." — the denominator shrinks.
"COUNT(*)." — count distinct users.
"Retention is returners over total users." — over the cohort.
"Today's cohort has 0% retention." — its day 1 hasn't happened.

databases-q16.testing: an atomic insert-or-update, plus a guard so replays and out-of-order messages are harmless.
databases-q16.trap: SELECT, then INSERT or UPDATE in application code: two workers both find no row and both insert.
databases-q16.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Read the tables "One table, inventory, keyed by SKU, with a quantity and an updated-at. Messages arrive from a queue, possibly twice and possibly out of order. Each should create the row or update it, and an older message must never replace newer data."
2 · Name the pattern "That's an upsert with a version guard. The upsert makes insert-or-update one atomic statement. The guard makes it safe to replay."
3 · Write it "Insert the row. On conflict on the SKU, do an update that sets the quantity and timestamp from the incoming row, with a where clause: only when the incoming timestamp is greater than the stored one."
4 · Trace it on data "Three messages. A newer one for an existing SKU updates it to nine. An older one arrives late and changes nothing. One for a new SKU inserts. Running all three again changes nothing."
5 · Variants and traps "The conflict target needs a unique constraint. And replace-style statements delete and reinsert, which wipes columns I didn't supply."
6 · How it performs "It's one index lookup and one write. For bulk loads I send many rows per statement."
Close "One atomic statement, and a comparison that makes old messages lose."

stages.name: Read the tables
stages.claim: a key, a value, a version
stages.html:
"The third column is what makes ordering decidable."

inventory(sku PRIMARY KEY, qty, updated_at)
sku qty updated_at
A1 5 2026-03-01
Property wanted Meaning
Upsert the row is created if missing, updated if present
Idempotent applying the same message twice leaves the same state
Order-safe a message older than the stored row is ignored

stages.name: Name the pattern
stages.html:
"Two separate ideas in one statement."

Pattern:INSERTUPDATE from the incoming row ─only if incoming version > stored versiondone
Clue in the question Pattern
"insert or update", "sync", "apply events" upsert
"replayed", "at-least-once", "out of order" a version or timestamp guard

stages.name: Write it
stages.html:
"excluded is the row that failed to insert." Run on SQLite 3.51; the same form runs on PostgreSQL.

INSERT INTO inventory(sku, qty, updated_at)
VALUES (?, ?, ?)
ON CONFLICT(sku) DO UPDATE
  SET qty = excluded.qty,
      updated_at = excluded.updated_at
WHERE excluded.updated_at > inventory.updated_at;

After three messages (below):

sku qty updated_at
A1 9 2026-03-05
B2 4 2026-03-05

stages.name: Trace it on data
stages.html:
"Each message, the path it takes, and the table afterwards." Run on the sample.

# Message Path Rows changed A1 after B2 after
1 A1, qty 9, 03-05 conflict → 03-05 > 03-01 → update 1 9, 03-05 —
2 A1, qty 2, 03-02 conflict → 03-02 > 03-05 is false → skip 0 9, 03-05 —
3 B2, qty 4, 03-05 no conflict → insert 1 9, 03-05 4, 03-05
1 again A1, qty 9, 03-05 conflict → 03-05 > 03-05 is false → skip 0 9, 03-05 4, 03-05

Message 2 is the late arrival. Without the WHERE, quantity would end at 2.

stages.name: Variants and traps
stages.html:
"INSERT OR REPLACE INTO inventory(sku, qty) VALUES ('A1', 9)." Run on the sample.

sku qty updated_at
A1 9 NULL

It deletes the old row and inserts a new one, so every column not supplied is lost, and delete triggers and cascades fire.

Trap What happens
SELECT, then INSERT or UPDATE in code two workers both see "missing"; one fails on the key or a duplicate appears
No unique constraint on the key there is no conflict to catch: every message inserts
REPLACE delete + insert: columns reset, cascades fire
Timestamps as the version clock skew between producers; equal timestamps
qty = qty + excluded.qty not idempotent: a replay adds twice
Dialect Form
PostgreSQL, SQLite INSERT … ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE … WHERE …
MySQL INSERT … ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE qty = IF(new.updated_at > updated_at, new.qty, qty), …
SQL Server, Oracle MERGE … WHEN MATCHED AND src.updated_at > tgt.updated_at THEN UPDATE … WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT

stages.name: How it performs
stages.html:
"The key's unique index does the work."

Design Effect
The unique index on sku detects the conflict; one seek
Many rows per statement fewer round trips and commits for bulk sync
Rows sorted by key within a batch concurrent batches take locks in the same order: fewer deadlocks
A monotonic version from the source no dependence on clocks

What breaks at scale: a skipped update still takes the row lock briefly; under heavy replay that is contention. Deduplicate in the consumer before the database when replays are common.

Fix layer: the statement for atomicity, the message design for the version.

followUps.question: "Check whether the row exists, then insert or update."
followUps.html:
Two workers can both pass the check.

Time Worker A Worker B
1 SELECT → no row SELECT → no row
2 INSERT
3 INSERT → key violation, or a duplicate if there's no constraint

followUps.question: 🧪 The row holds A1 = 9 at 03-05. A message A1 = 2 at 03-02 arrives. What is stored afterwards, and how many rows changed?
followUps.html:
Still 9 at 03-05; zero rows changed.

conflict on sku → evaluate WHERE excluded.updated_at > inventory.updated_at
'2026-03-02' > '2026-03-05' → false → no update          ← run on the sample: rowcount 0

followUps.question: Why is "set qty = 9" idempotent and "add 4 to qty" not?
followUps.html:
An absolute write lands in the same state however often it runs.

Message Applied once Applied twice
Set qty to 9 9 9
Add 4 9 13

A delta needs a processed-message id to be safe.

followUps.question: Timestamp or version number for the guard?
followUps.html:
A version number from the source of truth.

  • Timestamps: clocks disagree between machines, and ties are possible.
  • A sequence or log position per key: strictly increasing, no clocks.

followUps.question: A delete arrives, then a late update for the same key. What happens?
followUps.html:
The late update re-creates the row, unless deletes are remembered.

Fix:keep a tombstone (deleted_at, with its version)the guard compares against itpurge tombstones after the replay window

dontSay: "Select, then insert or update." — it races.
"REPLACE INTO." — it deletes the row first.
"Messages arrive in order." — not with retries and partitions.
"Exactly-once delivery handles it." — the write still has to be idempotent.

databases-q17.testing: keyset (cursor) pagination: seeking past the last row seen, with a unique tie-breaker and a matching index.
databases-q17.trap: a cursor on a non-unique column alone, which skips or repeats rows that share a value.
databases-q17.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Read the tables "One table, orders, shown newest first, a page at a time. With offset, the database reads and throws away every row before the page, so page ten thousand is slow. And if a row is inserted while someone is paging, they see a row twice."
2 · Name the pattern "The alternative is keyset pagination. I don't say 'skip N rows'. I say 'give me the rows after this one', where 'this one' is the last row of the previous page."
3 · Write it "I order by created-at and id, both descending. The next page is where the pair created-at, id is less than the pair from the last row, with a limit. The id is there because dates aren't unique."
4 · Trace it on data "Page one is orders seven, six and five. The cursor is the first of March, id five. The next page is everything below that pair: orders four and three."
5 · Variants and traps "The cost is that I can't jump to page fifty. It's next and previous only. And the sort key must be unique and immutable, or rows get skipped."
6 · How it performs "With an index on created-at and id, the query seeks straight to the cursor. The plan shows a search, where offset shows a scan."
Close "Remember the last row, seek past it, tie-break on the id."

stages.name: Read the tables
stages.html:
"OFFSET has two problems: work and drift."

orders(id, customer_id, amount, status, created_at)

page p of size s with OFFSET:
rows read    = (p − 1) × s + s
p = 10,000, s = 50  →  500,000 rows read to return 50        ← grows with the page number
Problem Effect
Work every page costs more than the last
Drift an insert or delete before the page shifts every later row by one

stages.name: Name the pattern
stages.claim: seek past the last row seen
stages.html:
"The cursor is a position in the sort order, not a count."

Pattern:order by (sort column, unique id)return a pagethe last row's key is the cursornext page: rows after the cursor
Clue in the question Pattern
"infinite scroll", "next page token", "deep pages are slow" keyset pagination
"jump to page 37" offset, or a different design

stages.name: Write it
stages.html:
"Compare the pair, not each column on its own." Run on SQLite 3.51 with the cursor ('2026-03-01', 5).

SELECT id, created_at FROM orders
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-03-01', 5)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 2;
id created_at
4 2026-02-14
3 2026-02-03

The first page has no WHERE. The engine-neutral form of the comparison (run on the sample: same rows):

WHERE created_at < '2026-03-01'
   OR (created_at = '2026-03-01' AND id < 5)

stages.name: Trace it on data
stages.html:
"All orders in the sort order, with the cursor marked." Run on the sample.

id created_at Page
7 2026-03-15 1
6 2026-03-09 1
5 2026-03-01 1 ← cursor = (2026-03-01, 5)
4 2026-02-14 2
3 2026-02-03 2
2 2026-01-20 3
1 2026-01-05 3

Drift, with OFFSET. Page 2 of size 2 is OFFSET 2. Run on the sample before and after a new order is inserted at the top:

Page 1 Page 2 (OFFSET 2)
Before the insert 7, 6 5, 4
After the insert (already shown: 7, 6) 6, 5 ← 6 appears again

The keyset query for "after (2026-03-09, 6)" returns 5, 4 either way.

stages.name: Variants and traps
stages.claim: the tie-breaker, and what you give up
stages.html:
"The cursor must identify exactly one position."

Trap What happens
Cursor on created_at alone, with < rows sharing the cursor's timestamp on the next page are skipped
The same, with <= they are repeated
A mutable sort column (updated_at, a score) a row that changes moves across pages: seen twice or never
Mixed directions (created_at DESC, id ASC) the row-value comparison doesn't apply; write the expanded form
A raw cursor in the URL encode it opaquely; validate it on the way back
OFFSET Keyset
Jump to page N yes no
Cost of a deep page grows constant
Stable under inserts no yes
Total count a separate query either way the same
Pick when small tables, admin screens feeds, APIs, exports, anything deep

Row-value comparison is supported by PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite; on SQL Server, write the expanded OR form.

stages.name: How it performs
stages.html:
"With an index on (created_at, id)." Plans produced by SQLite 3.51 on the sample.

keyset:  SEARCH orders USING COVERING INDEX ix (created_at<?)    ← seeks to the cursor
offset:  SCAN orders USING COVERING INDEX ix                     ← walks from the start, discarding
Design Effect
Index on the exact sort key (created_at, id) seek to the cursor, read LIMIT rows, stop
A filter as well (customer_id = ?) put the equality column first: (customer_id, created_at, id)
Fetch LIMIT + 1 tells you whether a next page exists without a count

What breaks at scale: sorting by a column with no index, or by a computed score. Keyset needs the order to exist in an index.

Fix layer: the API contract (a cursor, not a page number) and an index that matches the sort.

followUps.question: "OFFSET is fine if there's an index."
followUps.html:
The index gives the order; the skipped rows are still read.

With an index
OFFSET 500000 LIMIT 50 walks 500,050 index entries
Keyset seeks to one entry, reads 50

followUps.question: 🧪 A user is on page 1 (orders 7, 6). A new order arrives. They ask for page 2 with . What do they see?
followUps.html:
Orders 6 and 5: order 6 a second time.

before: 7 6 | 5 4 | …
after:  9 7 | 6 5 | …        ← everything shifted down by one; run on the sample

followUps.question: How do you page backwards?
followUps.html:
Flip the comparison and the order, then reverse the page.

Previous page:(created_at, id) > first row's keyORDER BY … ASC LIMIT nreverse in the application

followUps.question: The product wants "page 1 … 500" links. Now what?
followUps.html:
Offer what users actually use, and bound the rest.

  • Next and previous by cursor; a filter or search to jump.
  • If numbers are required: cap the depth, or precompute page boundaries.

followUps.question: How do you design the cursor for a public API?
followUps.html:
Opaque, validated and versioned.

Property Why
Opaque (encoded sort key + direction) clients can't depend on its shape
Signed or validated a tampered cursor can't read outside the caller's scope
Carries the sort and filters a cursor from one query can't be replayed against another
Has an expiry or a version the sort key can change later

dontSay: "LIMIT 50 OFFSET 500000." — it reads 500,050 rows.
"The cursor is the timestamp." — not unique.
"Keyset can jump to any page." — it can't; say so.
"I'd cache the whole result set." — for how many users, for how long?

databases-q18.testing: that you can explain why a lookup is a few page reads, and list the predicates that make the planner ignore the index.
databases-q18.trap: "an index makes queries faster", with nothing about writes, selectivity or functions on the column.
databases-q18.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "A B-tree index is a sorted copy of one or more columns, with a pointer back to each row, arranged as a shallow tree so any value is found in a few page reads."
2 · Mechanism "Each node is a disk page holding hundreds of keys. The root points to branches, branches to leaves, and the leaves hold the keys in order and are linked sideways. So a lookup walks three or four pages, and a range walks down once and then along the leaves."
3 · Where it breaks "It isn't used when the predicate can't use the sort order: a function on the column, a leading wildcard, a type mismatch. And the planner skips it on purpose when the predicate matches a large share of the table, because a scan is cheaper than that many random reads."
4 · How I'd use it "I index for the queries I have: the columns in where, join and order by. I confirm with the plan. And I count the cost, because every insert, update and delete maintains every index."
5 · Adjacent concept "It serves equality, ranges, prefixes and sorting. A hash index serves equality only. Full-text and array searches want an inverted index."
Close "Sorted, shallow, great for selective lookups and ranges; and never free on writes."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html:
"The table is in insertion order; the index is in key order."

Table (heap) Index on email
row 1 b@x.com a@x.com → row 3
row 2 c@x.com b@x.com → row 1
row 3 a@x.com c@x.com → row 2
Without the index With it
read every row, test each walk the tree to the key, follow the pointer

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
"The tree is shallow because each page holds many keys."

levels = ceil( log_fanout(rows) )
fanout 200, 1,000,000 rows      → 3 levels
fanout 200, 1,000,000,000 rows  → 4 levels            ← a thousand times the rows, one more page read
binary tree, 1,000,000,000 rows → 30 levels

The fan-out of 200 is illustrative; it depends on key size and page size.

Operation Path
Equality root ─▶ branch ─▶ leaf ─▶ row
Range walk down to the start ─▶ follow the leaf links ─▶ stop at the end
ORDER BY the key read the leaves in order: no sort
Insert find the leaf, add the key; a full page splits in two

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
"Each predicate, and the plan it gets." Plans produced by SQLite 3.51 on the sample, with indexes on users(email) and orders(created_at).

Predicate Plan Why
email = 'a@x.com' SEARCH … USING INDEX (email=?) equality
created_at >= … AND created_at < … SEARCH … (created_at>? AND created_at<?) range
ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 3 SCAN orders USING INDEX reads the index in order; no sort
email GLOB 'a@*' (a prefix) SEARCH … (email>? AND email<?) a prefix is a range
email LIKE '%x.com' SCAN users a leading wildcard: no starting point
lower(email) = 'a@x.com' SCAN users the index stores email, not lower(email)
substr(created_at,1,7) = '2026-02' SCAN orders a function on the column

After CREATE INDEX … ON users(lower(email)) the lower(email) query becomes SEARCH users USING INDEX ix_lower (<expr>=?).

Also not used when Reason
The predicate matches much of the table many random row reads cost more than one sequential scan
Types don't match (a string column compared with a number) an implicit cast is a function on the column
Statistics are stale the planner misjudges the selectivity
The leading column of a composite index is missing see composite-index

stages.name: How I'd use it
stages.claim: from the queries, checked by the plan
stages.html:
"An index is a trade: read speed for write work."

Order:list the slow queriesread their plansindex the WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY columnsplan againmeasure writes
Index for Don't index
Selective filters a boolean or a status with three values, on its own
Foreign keys used in joins columns no query filters or sorts by
Sort keys of paged lists small tables: a scan is one page
Cost of each index Where it shows
Every write updates it insert and update latency
Memory indexes compete for the buffer cache
Page splits and bloat random keys (UUID v4) scatter inserts

Measure: the plan, index usage counters (unused indexes are pure cost), write latency before and after.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
"B-tree is the default because it does the most kinds of query."

Index Serves Pick when
B-tree =, <, >, BETWEEN, prefix, ORDER BY almost always
Hash = only pure key lookups, in memory
Inverted (GIN, full-text) "contains this word or element" text search, arrays, JSON keys
Spatial (GiST, R-tree) "within", "overlaps", nearest geometry, ranges
Block range (BRIN) ranges on naturally ordered data huge append-only tables
LSM-tree (a storage structure) write-heavy workloads see btree-or-lsm

Fix layer: indexes, chosen from the query shapes.

followUps.question: "Index every column in the WHERE clauses, to be safe."
followUps.html:
Each one slows every write, and most won't be chosen.

Indexes on a table Write cost Benefit
The few the queries need small used
One per column every insert updates all of them the planner uses one or two

followUps.question: 🧪 A table has an index on ; 95% of rows are 'active'. Does  use it?
followUps.html:
No, and that's the right decision.

1,000,000 rows × 95% = 950,000 index entries → 950,000 row fetches in key order (random pages)
full scan            = every page once, sequentially

WHERE status = 'failed' on the remaining few percent would use it. A partial index on the rare values is smaller still.

followUps.question: Why a B-tree and not a binary tree or a hash table?
followUps.html:
It's built for pages and for ranges.

Structure Page reads for one key in a billion Ranges
Binary tree about 30 yes
B-tree about 4 yes
Hash 1–2 no

followUps.question: What's the difference between a clustered and a secondary index?
followUps.html:
Whether the leaves hold the row itself.

Clustered Secondary
Leaves hold the whole row the key and a pointer (or the primary key)
Per table one many
Engines InnoDB: the primary key is clustered PostgreSQL: all indexes are secondary to a heap

followUps.question: How do you find indexes to remove?
followUps.html:
From usage statistics over a full business cycle.

Signal Action
Zero scans in the usage counters candidate to drop
A prefix of another index ((a) beside (a, b)) redundant
Used only by a monthly job keep, or build it for the job

dontSay: "Indexes make queries faster." — which queries, at what write cost?
"It has an index, so it's used." — not with a function or a leading wildcard.
"A full scan is always bad." — it's right when most rows match.
"Index everything." — every write pays.

databases-q19.testing: the leftmost-prefix rule, the equality-then-range ordering, and that you'd confirm with a plan.
databases-q19.trap: ordering the columns by "most selective first", whatever the queries look like.
databases-q19.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "A composite index is one B-tree sorted by the first column, then by the second within each value of the first. It's like a phone book sorted by surname, then first name."
2 · Mechanism "So a query can use it from the left. Customer id alone: a seek. Customer id and a range on created-at: a seek on both. Created-at alone: the index can't be entered, because dates are only sorted within each customer."
3 · Where it breaks "It breaks in three ways: the leading column is missing from the predicate, a function wraps the column, or a range on an earlier column stops later columns from being used for seeking."
4 · How I'd use it "The rule I design by is equality columns first, then one range column, then columns for sorting. And I check the plan, because that's the only proof the index is used."
5 · Adjacent concept "If the index also holds every column the query selects, the table isn't read at all. That's a covering index."
Close "Usable from the left; equality first, then the range; and the plan decides."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html:
"The index is one sorted list of pairs."

customer_id created_at → row
1 2026-01-05 order 1
1 2026-01-20 order 2
1 2026-02-14 order 4
1 2026-03-15 order 7
2 2026-02-03 order 3
2 2026-03-01 order 5

Within customer 1 the dates are in order. Across the whole index they are not: 2026-02-03 comes after 2026-03-15.

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
"What each predicate gets from the index." Plans produced by SQLite 3.51 on the sample, with the index on (customer_id, created_at).

Query predicate Plan line Verdict
customer_id = 1 AND created_at > … SEARCH … USING INDEX (customer_id=? AND created_at>?) seek on both
customer_id = 1 SEARCH … USING INDEX (customer_id=?) seek on the prefix
created_at > … SCAN orders full scan
SELECT customer_id, created_at … WHERE customer_id = 1 SEARCH … USING COVERING INDEX (customer_id=?) index only
substr(created_at,1,7) = '2026-02' SCAN orders function on the column
Seek path:find the first entry for customer 1within it, find the first date after the boundread forward until the customer changes

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
"Three ways a correct-looking index goes unused."

Break Why Fix
The leading column isn't in the WHERE the second column isn't sorted globally a second index, or a different column order
A function or cast on the column the index stores the raw value rewrite as a range, or an expression index
A range on the first column, equality on the second after the range, the index is only useful as a filter put the equality column first
Low selectivity reading most of the table through an index is slower than a scan let it scan

stages.name: How I'd use it
stages.html:
"I order the columns from the query, and prove it with the plan."

Rule:equality columnsone range columnsort columnsincluded columns for covering
query: WHERE customer_id = 1 AND created_at > '2026-02-01' ORDER BY created_at

no index:                SCAN orders
                         USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY          ← scan, then sort
index (created_at):      SEARCH … USING INDEX (created_at>?)   ← seeks on the date only
index (customer_id,
       created_at):      SEARCH … USING INDEX (customer_id=? AND created_at>?)
                                                               ← seeks on both; already in order, no sort

All three plans were produced on the sample. The third also removes the sort, because the index returns rows already ordered by date within the customer.

Measure before adding: every index is paid for on every insert, update and delete.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
"If the index has every column the query needs, the table is never touched."

Ordinary index Covering index
Reads index, then the row index only
Plan says index scan index-only scan (PostgreSQL) / USING COVERING INDEX (SQLite)
Cost — a wider index: more write work and memory
PostgreSQL — INCLUDE (col) adds payload without widening the key

SELECT * defeats it: the query now needs columns the index doesn't hold.

followUps.question: "Put the most selective column first."
followUps.html:
Order by how the queries filter, not by selectivity alone.

Query Best order
a = ? AND b > ? (a, b), even if b is more selective
a = ? AND b = ? either; pick the one other queries also lead with

A range in the first position stops the second column from seeking.

followUps.question: 🧪 With an index on , can  across all customers avoid a sort?
followUps.html:
No.

index order: (1, Jan) (1, Feb) (1, Mar) (2, Feb) (2, Mar) …
needed:      Jan, Feb, Feb, Mar, Mar …        ← dates are ordered only within a customer

That query wants an index that leads with created_at.

followUps.question: Do I need a separate index on  as well?
followUps.html:
No. The composite index already serves it.

  • (customer_id, created_at) covers every query that leads with customer_id.
  • A separate (customer_id) index is redundant write cost.

followUps.question: How do you know the index is actually used in production?
followUps.html:
From the plan and from usage statistics.

Evidence Tells you
EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the real query which index, and actual rows
Index usage counters indexes that are never scanned: candidates to drop

followUps.question: A table has fourteen indexes. What's your concern?
followUps.html:
Write cost and overlap.

Problem Check
Every write maintains all fourteen insert and update latency
Prefix duplicates (a) next to (a, b)
Never used zero scans in the usage counters

dontSay: "The index has that column, so the query uses it." — only from the left.
"Most selective column first." — equality before range, by the queries.
"I added an index and it's faster." — show the plan.
"More indexes can't hurt." — every write pays for each one.

databases-q20.testing: that you know the second step of an index lookup (fetching the row) and how to remove it.
databases-q20.trap: adding every selected column to every index, and paying for it on each write.
databases-q20.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "A covering index is one that contains every column a query needs. The database answers from the index alone and never reads the table row."
2 · Mechanism "A normal index lookup has two steps: find the entries in the index, then fetch each row from the table. That second step is a random read per row. If the select list and the filters are all in the index, the second step disappears."
3 · Where it breaks "It stops covering the moment the query asks for one more column, which is why select star defeats it. And a wider index costs more on every write and takes more memory."
4 · How I'd use it "I use it for a few hot, narrow queries: a list endpoint, a count, an existence check. The plan tells me it worked: index-only scan on PostgreSQL, covering index on SQLite."
5 · Adjacent concept "On PostgreSQL and SQL Server, include columns add payload to the leaves without making the key wider."
Close "All needed columns in the index, so no trip to the table."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html:
"Covering is a property of an index and a query together."

Query needs Index holds Covering?
customer_id, created_at (customer_id, created_at)
customer_id, created_at, amount (customer_id, created_at) amount is only in the table
customer_id, created_at, amount (customer_id, created_at, amount)

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
"Two steps become one."

Ordinary:seek in the indexfor each entry, fetch the row from the tablereturn
Covering:seek in the indexreturn

Plans produced by SQLite 3.51 on the sample, with an index on (customer_id, created_at):

Query Plan
SELECT created_at … WHERE customer_id = 1 SEARCH orders USING COVERING INDEX ix (customer_id=?)
SELECT COUNT(*) … WHERE customer_id = 1 SEARCH orders USING COVERING INDEX ix (customer_id=?)
SELECT created_at, amount … WHERE customer_id = 1 SEARCH orders USING INDEX ix (customer_id=?)
SELECT * … WHERE customer_id = 1 SEARCH orders USING INDEX ix (customer_id=?)

After adding (customer_id, created_at, amount), the third query becomes SEARCH orders USING COVERING INDEX ix2 (customer_id=?).

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.claim: one more column, and the write cost
stages.html:
"Covering is fragile and not free."

Break Why
SELECT * asks for columns the index doesn't hold
A new column added to the query later silently back to index + row fetch
PostgreSQL: pages not marked all-visible the index-only scan still visits the heap to check row visibility; vacuum keeps the visibility map current
Wide indexes more pages to write, cache and replicate
Frequently updated columns in the index each update rewrites the index entry 
row fetches saved  = rows returned per query × queries per second
cost added         = wider index entries on every insert and on updates to those columns

stages.name: How I'd use it
stages.html:
"I cover queries that return many rows from few columns."

Good candidate Poor candidate
A list endpoint: ids, titles, dates a detail page that needs the whole row
COUNT, EXISTS, MIN/MAX on the key queries returning one row: one fetch is cheap
A join that needs only the key and one value columns that change on most updates
Check:write the query with an explicit column listbuild the indexread the planmeasure reads per execution and write latency

Measure: heap fetches (PostgreSQL reports them per index-only scan), buffer reads, and insert latency before and after.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
"Key columns order the index; included columns only ride along."

Key column INCLUDE column
Used for seeking and sorting yes no
Stored in every level of the tree the leaves only
Supported by all engines PostgreSQL 11+, SQL Server
Engine What "the index already has it" means
MySQL InnoDB every secondary index carries the primary key, so it covers SELECT pk for free
InnoDB primary key clustered: the leaf is the row, so it covers everything
PostgreSQL a heap plus secondary indexes; index-only scans depend on the visibility map

Engine behaviour as generally documented; I'd confirm against the version in use.

Fix layer: indexes, sized to the select list.

followUps.question: "Put every column the table has into the index, so everything is covered."
followUps.html:
That's a second copy of the table, maintained on every write.

Narrow covering index "Everything" index
Size a fraction of the table about the table
Write cost small close to doubling the write

followUps.question: 🧪 The index is . Is  covered?
followUps.html:
No. amount forces a row fetch.

plan: SEARCH orders USING INDEX ix (customer_id=?)            ← no "COVERING"; run on the sample
add amount to the index → USING COVERING INDEX ix2

followUps.question: Why does SELECT * hurt here?
followUps.html:
It widens what the query needs to every column.

  • No index covers it short of the clustered one.
  • Name the columns, and the planner can answer from an index.

followUps.question: Key column or INCLUDE column?
followUps.html:
Key if you filter or sort by it; include if you only return it.

Column is used in Put it in
WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY the key
only the SELECT list INCLUDE

followUps.question: The index-only scan on PostgreSQL still shows many heap fetches. Why?
followUps.html:
The pages aren't marked all-visible yet.

Cause:recent writesvisibility map bits clearedthe scan checks the heap for those pagesvacuum sets the bits again

On a table with heavy churn, tune autovacuum for it, or accept that the scan is only partly index-only.

dontSay: "A covering index covers the table." — it covers a query.
"Add all the columns." — that's a second table.
"SELECT * is fine with a covering index." — it defeats it.
"It's free once built." — every write maintains it.

databases-q21.testing: a method: the order to read a plan in, and the three or four signs that explain a slow query.
databases-q21.trap: reading the estimated cost as time, or reading EXPLAIN without ANALYZE and trusting the estimates.
databases-q21.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "A plan is the tree of operations the database chose for a query: how it reads each table, how it joins them, and where it sorts or aggregates. Explain shows the choice; explain analyze runs the query and shows what happened."
2 · Mechanism "I read it from the innermost nodes outward, because those run first and feed their parents. At each node I look at three things: the access method, the estimated rows, and with analyze, the actual rows and time."
3 · Where it breaks "The first thing I compare is estimated against actual rows. If they differ by orders of magnitude, the planner chose with bad information, and everything above that node is suspect."
4 · How I'd use it "Then I look for the expensive shapes: a sequential scan that returns few rows, a nested loop with a large outer side, a sort or hash that spills to disk, and a filter that discards most of what was read."
5 · Adjacent concept "The plan depends on statistics. If the estimates are off, I refresh statistics before I change the query or add an index."
Close "Inside out; estimates against actuals; then the node where the time goes."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.claim: the plan, and the two commands
stages.html:
"One shows the intention; the other shows the result."

Command Runs the query? Shows
EXPLAIN no the chosen plan with estimated cost and rows
EXPLAIN ANALYZE (PostgreSQL, MySQL 8.0.18+) yes the same plus actual rows, loops and time per node
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) (PostgreSQL) yes also pages read from cache and from disk
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN (SQLite) no the access path per table

EXPLAIN ANALYZE on an UPDATE or DELETE performs it. Wrap it in a transaction and roll back.

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
"Children feed parents. The deepest node runs first."

The same query on the sample, as SQLite 3.51 reports it:

query: revenue per customer for paid orders, highest first

SCAN o                                          ← reads all of orders
SEARCH c USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)    ← one key lookup per order row
USE TEMP B-TREE FOR GROUP BY                    ← groups in a temporary structure
USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY                    ← then sorts the groups
On each node, read It tells you
Access method scan, index seek, index-only
Estimated rows what the planner expected
Actual rows × loops what happened; multiply the two
Time cumulative: a parent includes its children
Filter / rows removed how much was read and thrown away

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
"A wrong estimate is the root of most bad plans."

node:  Index Scan on orders   (rows=12)   (actual rows=480,000)       ← illustrative
ratio: 480,000 / 12 = 40,000× under-estimated
effect: the parent chose a nested loop, expecting 12 iterations
Estimate is wrong because Fix
Statistics are stale analyse the table
Columns are correlated (city and postcode) extended or multi-column statistics
A function or cast hides the column rewrite the predicate
Skewed values more detailed statistics; a plan per value class
Trap in reading Reality
"Cost is milliseconds" cost is an abstract unit for comparing plans
"Actual rows = 100" per loop; with loops = 5,000 that's 500,000
"The top node is slow" its time includes everything below it

stages.name: How I'd use it
stages.html:
"What I look for, and what each means."

Shape in the plan Usually means Next step
A sequential scan returning few rows a missing or unusable index index the predicate; check for a function on the column
Rows removed by filter ≫ rows returned the index finds too much, then filters a better-matched composite index
A nested loop with a large outer side a bad estimate picked the wrong join fix the estimate
A sort or hash spilling to disk the working set outgrew memory reduce rows earlier; then memory
A sort feeding a LIMIT no index in the sort order index the ORDER BY
The same subplan executed per row a correlated subquery rewrite as a join
Method:find the node with the most self-timecompare its estimate with actualchange one thingplan again

On the sample, an index on orders(customer_id, status, amount) changes the first line to SCAN o USING COVERING INDEX ix_o: the table is no longer read, and the two temporary B-trees remain.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
"The planner is a cost model fed by statistics."

Inputs:table and column statistics + available indexes + configurationcandidate planslowest estimated cost wins
Statistic Used for
Row count, pages scan cost
Distinct values, most common values, histogram selectivity of a predicate
Correlation with physical order index range scan cost

So a plan can change with no deploy: the data and its statistics changed. That's query-suddenly-slow.

Fix layer: statistics first, then indexes, then query shape.

followUps.question: "The cost went from 9,000 to 1,200, so it's seven times faster."
followUps.html:
Cost is the planner's estimate in its own units, not time.

Cost Actual time
From EXPLAIN EXPLAIN ANALYZE
Is a model's guess a measurement

followUps.question: 🧪 A node shows "actual rows=40 loops=2500". How many rows did it produce?
followUps.html:
100,000.

rows per loop × loops = 40 × 2,500 = 100,000

The node is the inner side of a nested loop that ran 2,500 times.

followUps.question: Is a sequential scan always a problem?
followUps.html:
No. It's right for small tables and for predicates that match much of the table.

  • Worry when it reads a million rows to return ten.
  • Don't when it returns most of what it reads.

followUps.question: How do you get the plan of a query that was slow last night?
followUps.html:
It has to be captured when it happens.

Tool Captures
Automatic plan logging for slow statements (PostgreSQL auto_explain) the actual plan at the time
Query statistics views which statements, how often, how long
Re-running it today today's plan, which may differ

followUps.question: The plan is right in staging and wrong in production. Why?
followUps.html:
Different data, so different statistics, so a different plan.

Difference Effect
Volume a scan that's fine on 10,000 rows
Skew one tenant with half the rows
Parameters a generic plan cached for a typical value

Test plans on production-shaped data, with the parameter values that hurt.

dontSay: "I read it top to bottom." — execution starts at the leaves.
"The cost is the time." — it's a unit for comparison.
"Sequential scans are bad." — sometimes they're the best plan.
"I ran EXPLAIN." — with ANALYZE, or you saw only estimates.

databases-q22.testing: that you can name the anomalies, know the defaults differ by engine, and know the application must retry at the strict levels.
databases-q22.trap: assuming "repeatable read" means the same thing on every engine, or that the default level prevents lost updates.
databases-q22.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "An isolation level says which effects of other running transactions mine is allowed to see. Each level is defined by the anomalies it still permits."
2 · Mechanism "There are four standard levels. Read uncommitted allows dirty reads. Read committed stops those and still allows non-repeatable reads and phantoms. Repeatable read gives me a stable view of rows I've read; the standard still allows phantoms. Serializable allows none: the result must match some one-at-a-time order."
3 · Where it breaks "Two things catch people. Defaults differ: PostgreSQL defaults to read committed, MySQL's InnoDB to repeatable read. And PostgreSQL's repeatable read is snapshot isolation, which has no phantoms and still allows write skew."
4 · How I'd use it "I stay on the default and protect each invariant explicitly: an atomic update, a row lock, or a version column. For an invariant that spans several rows, I use serializable for that transaction, and the application retries when it's told to."
5 · Adjacent concept "Underneath, most engines implement this with multi-version concurrency control, so readers and writers don't block each other."
Close "Name the anomaly, pick the lowest level or lock that prevents it, and retry on failure."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.claim: levels are defined by what they allow
stages.html:
"Four anomalies, in plain words."

Anomaly What happens
Dirty read I read a change another transaction hasn't committed, and it rolls back
Non-repeatable read I read a row twice and get two different values
Phantom I run the same range query twice and get a different set of rows
Lost update two transactions read, modify and write; one overwrites the other
Write skew two transactions each read a set, each write a different row, and together break a rule

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
"The SQL standard's table, plus the two anomalies it doesn't list."

Level Dirty read Non-repeatable read Phantom Lost update Write skew
Read uncommitted possible possible possible possible possible
Read committed — possible possible possible possible
Repeatable read (standard) — — possible engine-dependent possible
Serializable — — — — —
Engine Default Note
PostgreSQL read committed its repeatable read is snapshot isolation: no phantoms; a concurrent update of the same row fails and must be retried
MySQL InnoDB repeatable read uses gap locks to block many phantoms

Engine behaviour as generally documented; I'd confirm against the version in use.

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
"A lost update at read committed, as two sessions." PostgreSQL-style read committed.

Time Session A Session B
1 SELECT stock → 5
2 SELECT stock → 5
3 UPDATE … SET stock = 4 (5 − 1)
4 commit
5 UPDATE … SET stock = 4 (5 − 1)
6 commit
Result: stock = 4, two items sold

Write skew at snapshot isolation. Rule: at least one doctor on call.

Time Session A (Alice) Session B (Bob)
1 count on call → 2 count on call → 2
2 "2 > 1, I can leave": sets Alice off call "2 > 1, I can leave": sets Bob off call
3 commit commit
Result: nobody on call

Neither wrote a row the other wrote, so a snapshot sees no conflict. Only serializable catches it.

stages.name: How I'd use it
stages.claim: protect the invariant, not the whole workload
stages.html:
"I pick the smallest tool that prevents the specific anomaly."

Invariant Tool
A counter or balance on one row an atomic statement: UPDATE … SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0
Read, decide, then write one row SELECT … FOR UPDATE, or a version column with a check
A rule across several rows (on call, no overlapping bookings) serializable for that transaction, or a constraint that encodes the rule
A report that must be self-consistent repeatable read / a snapshot
At serializable:runcommitretry the whole transactioncommit

The retry is the application's job. A strict level without a retry loop turns anomalies into errors that reach users.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
"Isolation levels are the contract; MVCC is how most engines keep it."

Lock-based MVCC
Readers and writers block each other don't block each other
A reader sees the current row, when it can get a lock a snapshot of committed versions
Cost waiting dead row versions to clean up

What each level means in practice is "which snapshot do I read from, and when is it taken": per statement at read committed, per transaction at repeatable read.

Fix layer: the transaction design in the application, backed by constraints in the database.

followUps.question: "We use transactions, so concurrent updates are safe."
followUps.html:
A transaction gives atomicity. Isolation is a separate setting, and the default allows lost updates.

Belief Reality at read committed
"Read then write in a transaction is safe" two transactions can both read 5 and both write 4
"The database will detect it" not at that level

followUps.question: 🧪 In the stock example, both sessions run  with no SELECT first. Result?
followUps.html:
3. No update is lost.

A: stock = stock − 1  → 4, commit
B: waits for A's row lock, re-reads the committed value 4, → 3

The read and the write are one statement, so there's no gap for another transaction to slip into.

followUps.question: Why not run everything at serializable?
followUps.html:
It costs throughput and requires retries everywhere.

  • More aborts under contention.
  • Every transaction needs a retry loop.
  • Most work doesn't have a cross-row invariant to protect.

followUps.question: What's the difference between a non-repeatable read and a phantom?
followUps.html:
One is about a row changing; the other about the set of rows changing.

Non-repeatable read Phantom
Second read differs because an existing row was updated a row was inserted or deleted in the range
Stopped by repeatable read serializable (or snapshot / gap locks, by engine)

followUps.question: How do you find isolation bugs before production?
followUps.html:
By testing the invariant under concurrency, not the code path alone.

Technique Finds
Concurrent tests that run the same operation in parallel and assert the invariant lost updates, write skew
A constraint that encodes the rule violations become errors, whatever the code does
Serialisation-failure and deadlock rates in monitoring contention that needs redesign

dontSay: "Repeatable read prevents phantoms." — by the standard it doesn't; by engine it varies.
"The default level is safe." — it allows lost updates.
"Serializable everywhere." — with what retry logic?
"ACID means no anomalies." — isolation has levels.

databases-q23.testing: that you know readers see a snapshot built from row versions, and that old versions have to be cleaned up by something.
databases-q23.trap: "MVCC means no locks". Writers still lock rows against other writers.
databases-q23.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "MVCC is multi-version concurrency control. An update doesn't overwrite a row in place for everyone. The database keeps the old version as well, so each transaction reads a consistent snapshot."
2 · Mechanism "Every row version is stamped with the transaction that created it and the one that replaced it. A reader has a snapshot: the set of transactions that had committed when it started. It sees the newest version that its snapshot allows, and ignores the rest."
3 · Where it breaks "The benefit is that readers don't block writers and writers don't block readers. The cost is dead versions. Someone has to remove them: vacuum in PostgreSQL, purge of the undo log in InnoDB. And a long-running transaction pins old versions, so cleanup can't proceed and the table bloats."
4 · How I'd use it "So I keep transactions short, alert on the oldest open transaction, and make sure vacuum keeps up on the tables with heavy updates."
5 · Adjacent concept "The isolation level decides when the snapshot is taken: per statement at read committed, once per transaction at repeatable read."
Close "Versions buy concurrency; cleanup is the bill."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html:
"An update adds a version; it doesn't replace one."

Lock-based reads MVCC
A reader meets a row being updated waits for the writer reads the last committed version
A writer meets a row being read waits for the reader proceeds
Two writers on one row one waits one waits (still a lock)

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
"One row, three versions, and who sees which." PostgreSQL-style: each version records its creating and deleting transaction.

Version balance created by replaced by
v1 100 txn 90 (committed) txn 105
v2 70 txn 105 (committed) txn 112
v3 40 txn 112 (in progress) —
Reader Its snapshot Sees Why

Transaction 112 itself its own writes 40 you see your own changes
Visibility rule:created by a transaction in my snapshot ─and─ not replaced by one in my snapshotvisible
Engine Where old versions live Cleaned by

MySQL InnoDB in the undo log; the row is updated in place the purge thread
Oracle undo segments undo retention

Engine behaviour as generally documented; I'd confirm against the version in use.

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.claim: dead versions and the long transaction
stages.html:
"Cleanup can only remove versions that no snapshot can still see."

Time Session A (a report) Session B (the application) Dead versions
1 BEGIN; reads at repeatable read 0
2 (still open, idle) updates 1 million rows 1 million, pinned by A
3 (still open) updates them again 2 million, pinned
4 vacuum runs can remove nothing
5 COMMIT removable at the next vacuum
Cost Symptom
Bloat tables and indexes grow; scans read dead rows
Cleanup load vacuum I/O competing with queries
Long transactions "snapshot too old" (Oracle), undo growth (InnoDB), bloat (PostgreSQL)
Transaction id wraparound (PostgreSQL) forced, aggressive vacuum if ids aren't frozen in time
Write skew a snapshot can't see a concurrent change it never conflicts with

stages.name: How I'd use it
stages.html:
"I manage the two things MVCC depends on."

Practice Why
Short transactions; no user think-time inside one nothing pins old versions
A timeout on idle-in-transaction sessions a forgotten BEGIN can't block cleanup for hours
Long reports on a replica or a snapshot export their snapshot doesn't hold back the primary
Autovacuum tuned per hot table the default thresholds are too lazy for large, busy tables
Batch large updates each batch's versions become removable quickly

Measure: age of the oldest open transaction, dead-tuple counts and bloat per table, vacuum runs and duration, undo history length (InnoDB).

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
"MVCC is the mechanism; the isolation level picks the snapshot."

Isolation level Snapshot taken So
Read committed at the start of each statement two statements can see different data
Repeatable read / snapshot once, at the first statement the whole transaction sees one moment
Serializable (PostgreSQL SSI) one snapshot + tracking of read/write dependencies aborts a transaction that would break serial order

The anomalies each level allows are in isolation-levels.

Fix layer: transaction length in the application; cleanup settings in the database.

followUps.question: "With MVCC there are no locks."
followUps.html:
Readers don't lock. Writers still do.

Pair Blocks?
Reader and writer no
Writer and writer, same row yes
Schema change and anything yes

followUps.question: 🧪 A session ran  yesterday and never committed. Updates continue. What happens to the table?
followUps.html:
It grows, and vacuum can't shrink it.

oldest snapshot = yesterday
every version newer than that might still be needed by it → none can be removed
dead versions accumulate until that session ends

followUps.question: Why does a DELETE not free space straight away?
followUps.html:
It marks the version dead; other snapshots may still need it.

Lifecycle:livedead but visible to old snapshotsremovablespace reusable

followUps.question: How does InnoDB differ from PostgreSQL here?
followUps.html:
Where the old versions are kept.

PostgreSQL InnoDB
Update writes a new tuple in the table the row in place + an undo record
Old readers read the old tuple rebuild the old version from undo
Bloat shows as table and index size undo log (history list) length

followUps.question: How would you detect the long-transaction problem before it hurts?
followUps.html:
Alert on the cause, not the symptom.

Alert on Catches
Age of the oldest transaction the session pinning versions
Sessions idle in a transaction application bugs and forgotten consoles
Dead-tuple ratio per table cleanup falling behind

dontSay: "MVCC means no locking." — writers lock.
"Deleted rows are gone." — they're dead versions until cleanup.
"Vacuum is a maintenance nicety." — it's part of how MVCC works.
"A long read is harmless." — it pins every newer dead version.

databases-q24.testing: the cycle (two transactions, two locks, opposite order), that the database resolves it by killing one, and that consistent lock ordering prevents it.
databases-q24.trap: confusing a deadlock with a lock wait, or "fixing" it by raising a timeout.
databases-q24.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "A deadlock is a cycle of waiting. Transaction one holds a lock that two wants, and two holds a lock that one wants. Neither can proceed, and waiting longer won't help."
2 · Mechanism "The classic case is two transfers in opposite directions. One locks account A then asks for B; the other locks B then asks for A. The database keeps a wait-for graph, finds the cycle, and aborts one transaction as the victim."
3 · Where it breaks "It also comes from less obvious places: a batch updating rows in a different order from the application, an unindexed foreign key that locks more than expected, and gap locks in InnoDB."
4 · How I'd use it "Prevention is ordering: every code path takes locks in the same order, for example by ascending primary key. I keep transactions short, and I always retry the victim, because the database will sometimes pick one anyway."
5 · Adjacent concept "A lock wait is different: one transaction is simply slow and the other is queued behind it. That ends on its own; a deadlock doesn't."
Close "Same lock order everywhere, short transactions, retry the victim."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html:
"Four conditions must all hold; break one and there's no deadlock."

Condition In a database
Mutual exclusion a row lock is held by one writer
Hold and wait a transaction keeps its locks while asking for more
No pre-emption locks are released only at commit or rollback
Circular wait T1 waits for T2, T2 waits for T1 ← the one I can design out

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
"Two transfers, opposite directions."

Time T1: transfer A → B T2: transfer B → A
1 UPDATE accounts … WHERE id = 'A' A
2 UPDATE accounts … WHERE id = 'B' B
3 UPDATE … WHERE id = 'B' waits for T2
4 UPDATE … WHERE id = 'A' waits for T1
5 deadlock detected: T2 is rolled back
6 gets B, commits the application retries T2

The detector looks for a cycle in the wait-for graph. A sketch of that check:

def has_cycle(waits, start):
    seen, t = [], start
    while t in waits and t not in seen:
        seen.append(t); t = waits[t]
    return t in seen
print(has_cycle({"T1": "T2", "T2": "T1"}, "T1"))   # opposite order
print(has_cycle({"T1": "T2"}, "T1"))               # same order: a queue
# → True
# → False

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
"Most production deadlocks aren't the textbook transfer."

Source Why it deadlocks
Two code paths touching the same tables in different orders order A → B in the API, B → A in a batch job
Bulk UPDATE … WHERE id IN (…) with unordered ids two batches lock overlapping rows in different orders
An unindexed foreign key a parent delete or update scans and locks far more child rows than intended
Gap locks (InnoDB, repeatable read) two inserts into the same gap each wait for the other's gap lock
Lock upgrade two transactions hold a shared lock on a row and both ask for exclusive
Long transactions locks held longer means more chance to overlap

stages.name: How I'd use it
stages.html:
"With one lock order there's a queue, never a cycle."

Time T1: transfer A → B T2: transfer B → A
1 locks the lower id first: A
2 locks the lower id first: waits for A
3 B, updates both, commits
4 A, B, updates both, commits
Practice Effect
A fixed lock order (ascending primary key; parent before child) no circular wait
SELECT … FOR UPDATE … ORDER BY id up front all locks taken in order, before any work
Short transactions; no remote calls inside less overlap
Sort the rows of a batch by key concurrent batches don't cross
Index foreign keys and WHERE columns of updates fewer rows locked
Retry on the deadlock error (PostgreSQL 40P01, MySQL 1213) the victim succeeds the second time

Measure: deadlocks per minute, the deadlock log (it names both statements), lock-wait time, retries per transaction.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
"Three things that look alike in an error log."

Deadlock Lock wait Lock timeout
Shape a cycle a queue behind a slow holder a wait that exceeded the limit
Ends by itself? no yes, when the holder commits cut off by the timeout
Database action aborts a victim at once none errors the waiter
Fix lock ordering shorten the holder's transaction the same; the timeout is a guard

Fix layer: transaction design in the application; indexes so locks stay narrow.

followUps.question: "Increase the lock timeout so they stop failing."
followUps.html:
A deadlock isn't a timeout. Neither side will ever finish.

Setting Effect on a deadlock
A longer lock timeout none: the detector aborts a victim first
Disabling detection both wait until the timeout, then fail anyway

followUps.question: 🧪 Both transfers lock accounts in ascending id order. T1 moves A → B, T2 moves B → A, at the same instant. What happens?
followUps.html:
T2 waits for T1, then runs. No deadlock.

T1: lock A ✅ → lock B ✅ → commit
T2: lock A ⏳ (T1 holds it) → after T1 commits: lock A ✅ → lock B ✅ → commit
wait-for graph: T2 → T1 only      ← no cycle

followUps.question: How does the database choose the victim?
followUps.html:
By engine-specific rules, roughly "the cheapest to roll back".

  • InnoDB: the transaction that has modified the fewest rows.
  • PostgreSQL: the one whose wait triggered the check.
  • Either way: the application must be ready to be the victim.

followUps.question: Is it safe to retry automatically?
followUps.html:
Yes, if the whole transaction is retried and its side effects are inside it.

Safe Not safe
Re-run the entire transaction from the start re-run only the failed statement
Side effects are database writes an email or a payment call was made mid-transaction

followUps.question: Deadlocks jumped after yesterday's release. First three steps?
followUps.html:
Read the deadlock report, find the new lock order, fix the order.

Steps:the deadlock log names both statementsfind which one the release added or reorderedalign its lock order with the existing path, or add the missing index

Details in deadlocks-after-release.

dontSay: "Raise the timeout." — a cycle doesn't time out its way to success.
"Deadlocks mean the database is broken." — they're a normal outcome to handle.
"We don't need retries." — the detector will pick a victim.
"Use a table lock." — it trades deadlocks for no concurrency.

databases-q25.testing: that durability comes from an append-only log flushed at commit, and that the same log drives recovery, replication and CDC.
databases-q25.trap: "commit writes the data to the table files". It doesn't; it writes the log.
databases-q25.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "The write-ahead log is an append-only record of every change. The rule is in the name: a change is written to the log, and the log is flushed to disk, before the change is allowed to reach the data files."
2 · Mechanism "On commit, the database flushes the log records for that transaction and then acknowledges. The table pages are changed only in memory and written out later, in the background, at a checkpoint. After a crash, recovery replays the log from the last checkpoint: committed changes are redone, uncommitted ones are discarded."
3 · Where it breaks "It only holds if the flush is real. If the fsync is turned off, or the disk lies about it, a committed transaction can be lost. And the log has to be kept until it's no longer needed, so a stuck replica or replication slot can fill the disk."
4 · How I'd use it "In practice I leave synchronous commit on for anything that matters, put the log on fast storage, and monitor how much log is being retained."
5 · Adjacent concept "The same log is what replicas replay, what point-in-time recovery rolls forward, and what change data capture reads."
Close "One sequential log gives durability, crash recovery, replication and CDC."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html:
"Two places a change can be; only one has to be durable at commit."

The log The data files
Write pattern sequential append random page writes
Flushed at every commit later, at checkpoints
If lost in a crash committed work is lost nothing: rebuilt from the log

Why it's fast: one sequential flush covers many random page changes, and several commits can share one flush (group commit).

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
"The path of one commit, and what a crash leaves behind."

A sketch of redo recovery: two transactions, one committed, then a crash before any page reached the data files.

log, disk = [], {"A": 100, "B": 50}             # disk = data files
def write(txn, key, val): log.append((txn, key, val))   # log first
def commit(txn): log.append((txn, "COMMIT", None))      # fsync here
write(1, "A", 70); write(1, "B", 80); commit(1)
write(2, "A", 0)                                 # no commit, then crash
committed = {t for t, k, _ in log if k == "COMMIT"}
for t, k, v in log:                              # recovery: replay the log
    if k != "COMMIT" and t in committed:
        disk[k] = v                              # redo committed only
print(disk)
# → {'A': 70, 'B': 80}

Transaction 2's change to A never appears: it had no commit record.

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.claim: a flush that isn't, and a log that grows
stages.html:
"The guarantee is exactly as strong as the fsync."

Failure Cause Guard
A committed transaction is lost fsync disabled, or asynchronous commit, or a disk cache that acknowledges early keep sync on; storage that honours flushes
The disk fills with log a replica or a replication slot that stopped consuming; a failing archive command alert on retained log size
Long recovery after a crash checkpoints too far apart bound the checkpoint interval
I/O spikes a checkpoint writing everything at once spread checkpoints out
A torn page (half-written at the crash) a partial page write full-page images in the log (PostgreSQL), doublewrite buffer (InnoDB)
Setting Trade
Synchronous commit durable; each commit waits for a flush
Asynchronous commit faster; a crash can lose the last fraction of a second of commits, without corruption

stages.name: How I'd use it
stages.html:
"Three decisions and three numbers."

Decision Default I'd take
Sync or async commit sync for money and orders; async only for data I can lose or replay
Where the log lives fast, separate storage with a battery- or capacitor-backed cache
Archiving ship the log off the machine continuously: it's the basis of point-in-time recovery

Measure: log generated per second, retained log size (per replication slot), commit latency (it is mostly the flush), checkpoint duration.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
"Everything that needs 'the changes, in order' reads the same log."

Use How the log serves it
Crash recovery replay from the last checkpoint
Replication replicas receive and replay the log stream
Point-in-time recovery a base backup + archived log, replayed to a chosen moment
Change data capture a decoder turns log records into row-change events
Engine Name
PostgreSQL WAL
MySQL InnoDB redo log (crash recovery) + binlog (replication, CDC)
SQLite WAL mode, or a rollback journal

Fix layer: durability settings and storage; the application chooses sync or async per workload.

followUps.question: "COMMIT writes the changed rows to the table file."
followUps.html:
It flushes the log. The table pages follow later.

At commit On disk
Log records flushed
Table and index pages still only in memory, possibly for minutes

followUps.question: 🧪 The server loses power one millisecond after acknowledging a commit. No checkpoint has run. Is the change lost?
followUps.html:
No.

commit acknowledged ⇒ its log records were fsynced
restart → recovery replays the log from the last checkpoint → the change is redone

It would be lost only if the flush was skipped (async commit, fsync off, a lying disk).

followUps.question: What is a checkpoint for?
followUps.html:
It bounds recovery time and lets old log be recycled.

Checkpoint:write all dirty pages to the data filesrecord the log positionlog before it is no longer needed for crash recovery

followUps.question: When is asynchronous commit acceptable?
followUps.html:
When losing the last moment of commits is tolerable.

Fine Not fine
Click streams, metrics, caches that can be rebuilt payments, orders, anything acknowledged to a user as final

followUps.question: The primary's disk is filling with log files. What do you check?
followUps.html:
Who is making the database keep them.

Check Fix
An inactive replication slot drop it, or repair its consumer
A replica far behind fix the lag, or rebuild the replica
A failing archive command repair archiving; log is kept until it succeeds

dontSay: "Commit writes the table." — it writes the log.
"Turn off fsync for speed." — that removes durability.
"The log is just for crashes." — replicas, recovery and CDC read it too.
"Checkpoints make commits durable." — the log flush does.

databases-q26.testing: the cost shape of each algorithm, what input each needs, and that a wrong row estimate is what makes the planner pick badly.
databases-q26.trap: "nested loops are slow". With an index on the inner side and few outer rows, it's the fastest of the three.
databases-q26.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "These are the three ways a database physically joins two inputs. The SQL says what to join; the planner picks how, from its row estimates."
2 · Mechanism "A nested loop takes each row of the outer input and looks up matches in the inner one. A hash join builds a hash table on the smaller input, then probes it with the larger. A merge join walks two sorted inputs in step."
3 · Where it breaks "Nested loop is best when the outer side is small and the inner side has an index. Hash join is best for large, unsorted inputs with an equality condition, as long as the hash table fits in memory. Merge join is best when both sides are already sorted, for example from indexes."
4 · How I'd use it "So when a join is slow, I look at the estimates. The usual failure is a nested loop chosen for an expected ten rows that turned out to be half a million. I fix the estimate or the index and let the planner choose again."
5 · Adjacent concept "The same estimates also decide the join order, which often matters more than the algorithm."
Close "Few rows and an index: loop. Big and unsorted: hash. Already sorted: merge."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html:
"The same JOIN can run three ways."

You write The planner decides
which tables, on which condition the algorithm for each join
inner, left, semi, anti the order of the joins
which input is outer or build side

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
"What each one does with inputs of n and m rows."

Nested loop Hash join Merge join
Steps for each outer row, look up the inner side build a hash table on the smaller input; probe with the other walk two sorted inputs with two pointers
Cost shape n × m without an index; n × log m with one n + m n + m, plus sorts if not sorted
Needs an index on the inner side to be good memory for the hash table; an equality condition both inputs sorted on the join key
Conditions any (=, <, ranges) = only = (and some range forms)
First row arrives immediately after the build after any sort

A count of comparisons for 1,000 × 1,000 rows, sketched in Python:

import random
random.seed(1)
a = random.sample(range(5000), 1000); b = random.sample(range(5000), 1000)
nested = sum(1 for x in a for y in b)            # every pair
hashed = len(b) + len(a)                          # build + probe
sa, sb, i, j, merged = sorted(a), sorted(b), 0, 0, 0
while i < len(sa) and j < len(sb):                # two pointers
    merged += 1
    if sa[i] < sb[j]: i += 1
    elif sa[i] > sb[j]: j += 1
    else: i += 1; j += 1
print(nested, hashed, merged)
# → 1000000 2000 1788

The merge count excludes the two sorts it needed first.

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.claim: when each one wins and fails
stages.html:
"Pick-when and fail-when, side by side."

Wins when Fails when
Nested loop the outer side is small (tens or hundreds of rows) and the inner side has an index; LIMIT queries the outer side is large: one index lookup per row, millions of times
Hash join both sides are large and unsorted; analytics the hash table exceeds memory and spills to disk in batches
Merge join both sides arrive sorted from indexes; very large inputs the inputs need sorting first: the sorts dominate

stages.name: How I'd use it
stages.claim: fix the estimate, not the algorithm
stages.html:
"A bad join choice is nearly always a bad row estimate."

In the plan Likely cause Action
Nested loop, estimated 10 rows, actual 500,000 stale or missing statistics; correlated predicates analyse; extended statistics
Nested loop with a scan on the inner side no index on the join column index the foreign key
Hash join with "batches > 1" or disk usage the build side didn't fit in memory filter earlier; then raise the work memory
A sort feeding a merge join no index in join-key order an index, or let it hash
Order:actual planestimates against actuals at the joinfix statistics or the indexplan again

Hints or disabling an algorithm are a diagnostic, not a fix: they stop the planner adapting when the data changes.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
"With several tables, the order can matter more than the algorithm."

orders (10,000,000) ⋈ customers (100,000) ⋈ countries (200),  filter: country = 'IN'

good: filter countries → 1 row → its customers → their orders        ← small intermediate results
bad:  orders ⋈ customers first → 10,000,000 rows → then filter       ← illustrative sizes
The planner Because
Starts from the most selective input intermediate results stay small
Searches fewer orderings beyond a dozen or so tables the number of orders grows factorially

Engine note: PostgreSQL has all three algorithms. MySQL historically used nested loops only and added hash joins in 8.0.18. I'd confirm against the version in use.

Fix layer: statistics and indexes; the planner picks the algorithm.

followUps.question: "Nested loops are slow; force hash joins."
followUps.html:
For a few outer rows with an indexed inner side, the loop wins easily.

Query Best
One order and its five items nested loop: six index lookups
All orders joined to all items hash join

followUps.question: 🧪 The outer side has 500,000 rows; the inner side is looked up by index at about 4 page reads each. Roughly how many page reads?
followUps.html:
About two million, mostly random.

500,000 lookups × 4 pages = 2,000,000 page reads
a hash join reads each table once, sequentially

followUps.question: Why can't a hash join do ?
followUps.html:
A hash table answers "equal to", not "less than".

  • Equality: same hash, same bucket.
  • A range: matching rows are spread across every bucket.

followUps.question: What happens when the hash table doesn't fit in memory?
followUps.html:
It partitions both inputs to disk and joins them a batch at a time.

Spill:split both sides by hash into batcheswrite to temporary filesjoin each pair of batches in memory

Correct, and much slower. The plan shows the batch count.
