An index lookup returns 50 rows the same lookup returns 5 million
Fine a scan or a different index would be better

followUps.question: How do you tell waiting from working?
followUps.html:
From wait events and from the plan's own timings.

  • Execution time in the plan is small, total time is large: it was waiting.
  • Lock-wait and pool-wait metrics say on what.

followUps.question: How do you stop plan flips from being incidents?
followUps.html:
Make them visible and make the hot queries robust.

Guard Effect
Plan capture on slow queries diagnosis in minutes
Indexes that make the good plan obviously cheapest less room for the planner to switch
Load tests on production-sized, skewed data flips found before release

dontSay: "I'd add an index." — after reading the plan.
"Nothing changed, so it must be the database." — data and statistics changed.
"I'd increase the instance size." — that hides a bad plan for a while.
"It's fast when I run it." — with which parameter, on which data?

databases-q39.testing: that you recognise replication lag and the read-your-writes guarantee, and can fix it without sending every read to the primary.
databases-q39.trap: "make replication synchronous", or adding a sleep before the redirect.
databases-q39.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "This is almost always replication lag. The write went to the primary, the next page read from a replica that hadn't applied it yet. The guarantee that's missing is read-your-writes."
2 · Rule out the fakes "Before I blame the replica, I rule out the look-alikes: a cache serving the old value, the write not having committed yet, the browser or a CDN showing an old page, or the write having failed quietly."
3 · Confirm with evidence "Then I confirm: where did that read go, and how far behind was that replica at that moment? If the same read on the primary shows the new value, it's lag."
4 · Fix by experiment "The fix is to route that user's reads to the primary for a short window after they write, or to make the read wait until the replica has caught up to the write's log position. Other users can keep reading replicas."
5 · Validate "I validate with a test that writes and immediately reads, in a loop, while replicas are under load."
6 · Productionise "And I make it a property of the data layer: lag is monitored, lagging replicas leave the pool, and each read path declares what staleness it accepts."
Close "Eventual consistency for others is fine; a user must see their own write."

stages.name: Name it
stages.html:
"The write and the read took different paths."

Guarantee Meaning
Eventual consistency replicas converge, sometime
Read-your-writes I always see my own changes
Monotonic reads I never see time go backwards between two reads

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.claim: four other ways to see old data
stages.html:
"Each has a quick check."

Fake Check
An application cache with the old value read with the cache bypassed; was the key invalidated on write?
The write hadn't committed (the redirect fired first, or the commit is async) order of commit and response in the code and the trace
The write failed and the error was swallowed is the new value on the primary at all?
A browser, CDN or HTTP cache response headers; hard reload
A stale search index or read model which store does that page read from?

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.claim: where the read went, and the lag then
stages.html:
"Three facts settle it."

Evidence Tells you
The trace of the failing read which node served it
Replica lag at that time (seconds, or log-position difference) whether the replica could have had the write
The same query on the primary new value there → the write is fine, the read was stale
Lag pattern Likely cause
Always a little normal for asynchronous replication
Spikes during batch jobs a large transaction or bulk write being replayed
One replica much worse a slow disk, a long query blocking replay, an under-sized node
Growing without recovering the replica can't keep up with the write rate

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.claim: give the writer a consistent read
stages.html:
"Options, from the simplest."

Experiment How Why Best suited when
E1 · Read from the primary after a write set a marker (session, cookie) for a few seconds after a user writes; route their reads to the primary the simplest read-your-writes writes per user are occasional
E2 · Wait for the replica carry the write's log position; the read waits until the replica has replayed it, or falls back to the primary exact, and keeps the primary's read load low the engine exposes log positions (PostgreSQL LSN, MySQL GTID)
E3 · Return the written data the write response carries the new state; the next page renders from it no read needed at all simple forms
E4 · Reduce the lag fix the slow replica; break up large transactions makes the window smaller, never zero lag is abnormal
Not a fix:sleep(1) before the redirectworks until lag is 2 seconds

stages.name: Validate
stages.html:
"A test that fails when the guarantee is missing."

Check Before After
Write then immediate read, 1,000 times, same session measure stale reads 0
The same while a bulk job creates lag measure 0
Share of reads on the primary measure measure: it must stay small
Primary CPU measure measure

Validated with replicas deliberately lagged, because the bug only shows when they are.

stages.name: Productionise
stages.html:
"Each read says what it can tolerate."

Practice Detail
Lag monitored per replica, with an alert minutes of lag is an incident
Lagging replicas are removed from the read pool automatically, above a threshold
Read paths are classed "must be current" → primary; "seconds stale is fine" → replica
Critical reads never use a replica balances, permissions, anything that gates a write
Large transactions are batched they replay as one block and stall replicas

Fix layer: read routing in the data-access layer; replication health in operations.

followUps.question: "Make replication synchronous."
followUps.html:
It slows every write and still may not fix the read.

Synchronous replication
Every commit waits for a replica
A slow or down replica stalls writes
Read-your-writes only if "synchronous" means applied, not just received

followUps.question: 🧪 Replica lag is 800 ms. A user saves and the next page loads 200 ms later from that replica. What do they see?
followUps.html:
The old value.

write committed at t = 0
replica applies it at t ≈ 800 ms
read arrives at   t = 200 ms  → 200 < 800 → not yet applied → stale

followUps.question: Why not send all reads to the primary?
followUps.html:
It gives up the reason for having replicas.

  • Only the writer needs their own write, and only for a moment.
  • Everyone else can read slightly stale data from replicas.

followUps.question: A user refreshes twice and the value goes new, then old. What's that?
followUps.html:
A monotonic-read violation: two replicas at different positions.

Fix:pin the session to one replicacarry the highest log position seennever read behind it

followUps.question: What else breaks under replication lag, apart from this screen?
followUps.html:
Anything that reads and then decides.

Read from a replica, then… Risk
Check a balance or stock, then write a decision on old data
Check a permission a revoked user still passes
A background job picks up "new" rows misses rows not yet replicated

dontSay: "Add a short delay." — lag isn't bounded by your sleep.
"Make replication synchronous." — a heavy fix for a routing problem.
"Read everything from the primary." — then why have replicas?
"It's eventually consistent, that's expected." — not for the user's own write.

databases-q40.testing: that you know which statements lock the table and for how long, and that you split the change into steps that can each be rolled back.
databases-q40.trap: one ALTER TABLE … NOT NULL DEFAULT … plus one UPDATE of every row.
databases-q40.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "First I ask which engine and version, because what locks differs, and whether the value is a constant or computed."
2 · Constraints and numbers "The limits are lock time and replica lag. No statement may hold a blocking lock for more than a moment, and the backfill must not push replicas behind."
3 · Baseline design "So I expand, backfill, then contract. Add the column as nullable, which is a metadata change. Deploy code that writes it on every insert and update. Backfill old rows in small batches. Add the constraint last."
4 · Deep-dive "The backfill walks the primary key in small batches, one short transaction each, and pauses when replica lag rises. On PostgreSQL I add a check constraint as not valid, then validate it, which scans without blocking writes."
5 · Failure modes "The dangerous one is the lock queue. A schema change waiting behind a long transaction blocks every query behind it, so I set a lock timeout and retry."
6 · Evolve "Then it becomes a rule: every migration is expand and contract, checked in the pipeline."
Close "No step holds a long lock, and every step before the constraint can be undone."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
"Three answers change the plan."

Question Why it matters
Which engine and version? adding a column with a default is a metadata change on PostgreSQL 11+ and on MySQL 8.0 InnoDB (ALGORITHM=INSTANT); older versions rewrite the table
Is the value a constant or computed? a constant can be a default; a computed value needs a backfill
Do old application versions still write to the table? until they are gone, a NOT NULL constraint rejects their inserts
Are there replicas or CDC consumers? every backfilled row is replicated and emitted

Engine behaviour as generally documented; I'd confirm against the version in use.

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
"Two budgets, and the arithmetic of the backfill."

Budget Limit
Blocking lock on the table well under a second per statement
Replica lag stays inside the alert threshold throughout
Transaction size small enough that undo, the log and vacuum keep up 
rows              = 1,000,000,000            ← illustrative for a 500 GB table
batch             = 5,000 rows
batches           = 1,000,000,000 / 5,000    = 200,000
time per batch    = 0.2 s work + 0.3 s pause = 0.5 s
total             = 200,000 × 0.5 s          = 100,000 s ≈ 28 hours

So the backfill is a job that runs for a day or more, and must be resumable.

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
"Five steps; each one is short or non-blocking."

Step Lock Undo
1 · Add nullable brief exclusive, metadata only drop the column
2 · Deploy writers none roll the deploy back
3 · Backfill row locks, a batch at a time stop the job
4 · Validate allows reads and writes (PostgreSQL) drop the constraint
5 · Enforce brief point of no return for old application versions

Step 2 comes before step 3. Otherwise rows inserted during the backfill arrive empty and the job never finishes.

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
"Walk the primary key; commit per batch." Run on SQLite through Python.

import sqlite3
m = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
m.execute("CREATE TABLE accounts(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT)")
m.executemany("INSERT INTO accounts(email) VALUES (?)",
              [(f"u{i}@x.com",) for i in range(1, 11)])
m.execute("ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN email_domain TEXT")  # expand
last = batches = 0
while True:
    ids = [r[0] for r in m.execute(
        "SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id > ? ORDER BY id LIMIT 4", (last,))]
    if not ids: break
    m.execute("UPDATE accounts SET email_domain = substr(email, "
              "instr(email, '@') + 1) WHERE id BETWEEN ? AND ?",
              (ids[0], ids[-1]))
    m.commit(); last = ids[-1]; batches += 1   # one short transaction
left = m.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM accounts "
                 "WHERE email_domain IS NULL").fetchone()[0]
print(batches, "batches;", left, "rows left NULL")
# → 3 batches; 0 rows left NULL
Property How
Resumable the last id is saved; a restart continues from it
Throttled pause while replica lag or lock waits are above the limit
Idempotent re-running a batch sets the same values
No OFFSET the key range is seeked, so batch 200,000 costs the same as batch 1
The constraint, on PostgreSQL 12+:ADD CONSTRAINT … CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALIDVALIDATE CONSTRAINTSET NOT NULL (uses the validated check, so no second scan)drop the check

On MySQL: an online schema-change tool (gh-ost, pt-online-schema-change) copies to a shadow table and swaps it in.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.claim: the lock queue and the long transaction
stages.html:
"What turns a metadata change into an outage."

Failure Cause Guard
Every query on the table stalls the ALTER waits behind a long transaction, and everything queues behind the ALTER lock_timeout of a second or two, then retry
Replicas fall behind the backfill writes faster than they apply throttle on lag
The log or undo space fills one huge transaction commit per batch
Inserts fail after step 5 an old application version doesn't set the column confirm no old writers; a default as a safety net
CDC consumers are flooded a billion update events tell the owners; filter or pause

Measure during the run: lock waits, replica lag, rows left NULL, write latency on the table.

stages.name: Evolve
stages.claim: make it the only way to migrate
stages.html:
"The pattern outlives this one change."

Practice Detail
Expand and contract for every change renames, type changes and splits follow the same steps
A migration linter in CI rejects a blocking ALTER, a missing lock timeout, an unbatched UPDATE
Schema and code deploy separately the schema is always compatible with the previous and the next application version
A backfill framework resumable, throttled, observable; not a one-off script each time

Fix layer: migration process, enforced in the pipeline.

followUps.question: "Just run ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN … NOT NULL DEFAULT 'x'."
followUps.html:
Safe only for a constant default on an engine that stores it as metadata.

Case Result
Constant default, PostgreSQL 11+ / MySQL 8.0 instant fast; still needs a lock timeout
Computed value, or an older version a full table rewrite under a blocking lock

followUps.question: 🧪 The backfill uses . What happens by batch 100,000?
followUps.html:
Each batch reads and throws away every row before it.

batch 100,000: OFFSET = 100,000 × 5,000 = 500,000,000 rows skipped   ← to update 5,000
keyset:        WHERE id > last ORDER BY id LIMIT 5000                ← seeks straight there

followUps.question: Why add the constraint as NOT VALID first?
followUps.html:
It splits a long blocking step into a short one and a non-blocking one.

  • NOT VALID: enforced for new writes at once; no scan.
  • VALIDATE: scans existing rows while reads and writes continue.

followUps.question: How do you roll back?
followUps.html:
Every step before enforcement has a one-line undo.

Undo:stop the backfilldrop the constraintroll back the writersdrop the column

After SET NOT NULL, rolling the application back to a version that doesn't write the column fails.

followUps.question: How do you stop the next engineer from running the blocking version?
followUps.html:
The pipeline refuses it.

Guard Catches
A migration linter blocking statements, missing timeouts
A default lock timeout for the migration role a queue building behind a waiting ALTER
Migrations tested on a production-sized copy a rewrite that takes hours

dontSay: "I'd run the ALTER at night." — a blocking lock at 3 a.m. is still an outage.
"One UPDATE to fill it in." — one transaction over 500 GB.
"Adding a column is instant." — on which engine, with which default?
"We'll take a short maintenance window." — the question said zero downtime.

databases-q41.testing: that you separate a bad key from one big tenant from one hot key, and have a way to move data without downtime.
databases-q41.trap: adding more shards, which leaves the hot tenant or key exactly where it was.
databases-q41.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "This is skew. The shard key isn't spreading load evenly. There are three versions: a key that concentrates by design, like a timestamp; one very large tenant; or one extremely hot key."
2 · Rule out the fakes "First I check it's really uneven data or traffic, and not that one shard has a slower disk, a missing index, a stuck vacuum, or a bad query landing there."
3 · Confirm with evidence "Then I break the shard's load down by key. If one tenant is most of it, that's a whale. If it's the newest range, the key is monotonic. If it's one row, it's a hot key."
4 · Fix by experiment "The fix depends on which. A whale moves to its own shard through the directory. If it's bigger than a node, I split it by a second-level key. A monotonic key gets hashed or prefixed. A hot key gets a cache in front or is split into sub-keys."
5 · Validate "I validate by load per shard before and after, and by checking the share of queries that now cross shards."
6 · Productionise "Long term, I want per-tenant and per-key load visible, and rebalancing to be a routine online operation."
Close "Find what's hot, move or split that, and keep the map adjustable."

stages.name: Name it
stages.html:
"The same symptom, three causes."

Kind Looks like Cause
A monotonic key the newest shard is hot; it moves over time range-sharded on a timestamp or sequence
A whale one shard is hot permanently; one tenant dominates tenants differ in size by orders of magnitude
A hot key one row or partition takes most requests a celebrity account, a viral item, a global counter
Uneven placement one shard simply has more tenants growth after the last rebalance

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.html:
"A slow shard looks like a hot shard."

Fake Check
Slower hardware or a noisy neighbour same queries per second as the others, but higher latency
A missing or invalid index on that shard compare schemas and plans across shards
Maintenance (vacuum, backup, compaction) timing matches the spike
One bad query or a batch job pinned to it top statements on that shard
A failed replica sending its reads to the primary replica health

Split the claim: more requests than the others, or the same requests running slower?

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
"Group the hot shard's load by the shard key."

Finding Diagnosis
One tenant ≈ most of the rows or queries a whale
Load concentrated in the latest key range a monotonic key
One key's requests dwarf the rest a hot key
Evenly many tenants, just more of them placement drift

A simulation of a whale: 39 tenants of 100 rows and one of 6,000, hashed by tenant to 4 shards.

import hashlib
sh = lambda k, n=4: int(hashlib.md5(str(k).encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % n
t = {f"t{i}": 100 for i in range(1, 40)}; t["big"] = 6000
before, own, split = [0] * 4, [0] * 5, [0] * 4
for k, v in t.items():
    before[sh(k)] += v
    own[4 if k == "big" else sh(k)] += v              # whale on shard 4
    if k == "big":
        for p in range(60): split[sh(f"big:{p}")] += 100   # by project
    else: split[sh(k)] += v
print(before); print(own); print(split)
# → [6900, 1100, 1100, 800]
# → [900, 1100, 1100, 800, 6000]
# → [2200, 2700, 2500, 2500]

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.claim: move it, split it, or absorb it
stages.html:
"The fix follows the kind of skew."

Experiment How Why Best suited when
E1 · Isolate the whale move the tenant to a dedicated shard; flip its directory entry the other tenants stop sharing its load one tenant fits on one node
E2 · Split the whale shard inside the tenant by a second-level key (tenant_id, project_id) its load spreads over several shards the tenant has outgrown a node
E3 · Fix a monotonic key hash the key, or prefix it with a bucket writes stop piling onto the newest range range sharding on time or a sequence
E4 · Absorb a hot key cache reads; split a counter into N sub-keys and sum them one key can't be divided by sharding celebrity rows, global counters
E5 · Rebalance placement move some tenants off the full shard evens out drift no single dominant tenant

stages.name: Validate
stages.claim: per-shard load, and what it cost
stages.html:
"Evenness, and the price paid for it."

Check Before After
Queries per second, CPU and storage per shard measure measure
p99 latency on the hot shard measure measure
Share of queries touching more than one shard measure measure: splitting a tenant raises it
The moved tenant's error rate during cut-over — measure

Splitting the whale by project evens the load and makes that tenant's cross-project queries fan out. That trade is checked, not assumed.

stages.name: Productionise
stages.html:
"Hot shards should be seen coming."

Practice Detail
Load per shard, per tenant and per top key on a dashboard the whale is visible while it's growing
A directory (tenant → shard), not arithmetic a tenant moves by changing one row
An online move procedure copy ─▶ catch up ─▶ brief write pause ─▶ flip ─▶ clean up
Per-tenant rate limits one tenant can't starve its neighbours
A size threshold that triggers isolation the decision is made before the incident

Fix layer: routing (the directory) and data model (a second-level key for whales).

followUps.question: "Add more shards."
followUps.html:
The hot tenant still lands on exactly one of them.

4 shards 8 shards
The whale's shard 6,000+ rows 6,000+ rows
The others lighter lighter still

followUps.question: 🧪 In the simulation, what does the load look like after moving the big tenant to its own fifth shard?
followUps.html:
The original four are even; the fifth carries the whale alone.

[900, 1100, 1100, 800, 6000]        ← run above

That isolates the neighbours. It doesn't shrink the whale: if 6,000 is beyond one node, split it.

followUps.question: How do you move a tenant without downtime?
followUps.html:
Copy, catch up, pause briefly, flip.

Move:bulk copy to the targetreplicate changes until nearly caught uppause that tenant's writes for a momentfinal syncflip the directoryresumedelete the old copy later

followUps.question: A single counter row takes 30% of all writes. Sharding can't split a row. What do you do?
followUps.html:
Split the counter itself.

Technique How
Sharded counter N sub-counters; a write picks one at random; a read sums them
Buffered increments accumulate in memory or a cache; flush in batches
Append and aggregate insert events; compute the count asynchronously

followUps.question: How would you have avoided this at design time?
followUps.html:
By checking the key against the real size distribution.

Design check Catches
Simulate the key on production tenant sizes whales
Ask what the newest data's key looks like monotonic hot spots
A directory from day one the need to rehash everyone later

dontSay: "Add shards." — the hot key doesn't split.
"Re-hash everything." — a migration of all data to fix one tenant.
"Give that shard a bigger machine." — a stopgap; say so.
"The hash is uniform, so load is uniform." — tenants aren't the same size.

databases-q42.testing: that you look at what the connections are doing before raising the limit, and that you add up pools across the fleet.
databases-q42.trap: raising max_connections, which gives a slow database more work to do at once.
databases-q42.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "Hitting the connection limit is a symptom. Either the fleet is configured to ask for more connections than the database allows, or connections are being held too long, so they pile up."
2 · Rule out the fakes "First the arithmetic: pool size times instances, plus workers, cron jobs and admin tools, against the limit. If that sum is over the limit, it's configuration. Autoscaling often causes exactly that."
3 · Confirm with evidence "Then I look at what the sessions are doing. Active and running a query? Idle? Idle inside a transaction? Waiting on a lock? The state tells me the cause."
4 · Fix by experiment "If most are idle in transaction, the application holds connections across slow work: I fix that. If they're waiting on a lock, I find the blocker. If they're running slow queries, I fix the query. If the sum is just too large, I shrink the pools or put a pooler in front."
5 · Validate "I validate with a load test at peak, watching connection count, pool wait time and throughput."
6 · Productionise "Then I add timeouts, per-service connection budgets, and an alert well before the limit."
Close "Count the connections, see what they're doing, and fix the hold time before the limit."

stages.name: Name it
stages.claim: too many asked for, or held too long
stages.html:
"Two different problems behind one error."

Over-subscription Held too long
Cause pools × instances exceeds the limit each request keeps its connection for longer than its queries need
Appears when the fleet scales out, or a new service is deployed under load, or when something downstream slows
Sessions are mostly idle active, waiting, or idle in transaction 
connections needed ≈ requests per second × seconds each connection is held

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.html:
"Who can open connections, and how many."

web:        30 instances × pool 20   = 600
workers:    10 instances × pool 10   = 100
cron, migrations, admin, monitoring  ≈  20
total possible                       = 720      ← against max_connections = 300
Fake Check
Autoscaling added instances instance count at the time of the error
A new service or job with its own pool connections grouped by application name or user
A deploy doubling pools briefly (old and new instances together) timing matches a rollout
A connection storm after a restart every instance reconnecting at once
No pooling at all (a function or script per request) many short-lived sessions

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
"Group the sessions by state." On PostgreSQL this is pg_stat_activity; on MySQL, the process list.

Most sessions are Means Go to
Idle the pools are simply too large in total shrink pools; a pooler
Idle in transaction the application opened a transaction and is doing something else: a remote call, slow code, a leak fix the hold time
Active, same slow query a query regression is holding connections fix the query
Waiting on a lock one blocker; everyone queues behind it find and fix the blocker
Active, CPU saturated the database is doing more than it can reduce concurrency
Also look at Why
Connections by client address and application which service is the heavy one
Age of the oldest transaction a stuck one upstream of the queue
Pool metrics on the application side wait time and leak warnings

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.claim: shorten the hold, then cap the total
stages.html:
"One change at a time, in this order."

Experiment How Why Best suited when
E1 · Release connections sooner no remote calls inside a transaction; close transactions promptly; fix leaks the same load needs fewer connections sessions are idle in transaction
E2 · Fix the slow query or the blocker the plan; the blocking session each connection is busy for less time sessions are active or waiting
E3 · Right-size the pools pool per instance = budget ÷ maximum instances the fleet can't exceed the limit sessions are idle
E4 · A proxy pooler PgBouncer, RDS Proxy, ProxySQL in transaction mode many clients share few server connections many instances, serverless
E5 · Raise the limit only with memory and CPU headroom shown last resort the database is genuinely under-used 
hold time is the lever:
400 rps × 0.025 s = 10 connections
400 rps × 0.525 s = 210 connections      ← the same traffic, with a 500 ms call inside the transaction

stages.name: Validate
stages.claim: at peak, with the fleet scaled out
stages.html:
"The limit must hold at the worst case."

Check Before After
Peak connections against the limit measure measure
Pool acquire time, p99 measure measure
Throughput and latency measure measure: a smaller pool often improves both
Sessions idle in transaction measure near zero
Behaviour with instances at the autoscaling maximum — measure

stages.name: Productionise
stages.html:
"So it can't creep back."

Practice Detail
A connection budget per service the sum, at maximum scale, stays under the limit with headroom
Reserved connections for admins you can still log in during the incident
Timeouts statement, lock and idle-in-transaction timeouts on the database; acquire timeout in the pool
Alert at about 80% of the limit time to act
Pool size reviewed with autoscaling limits the two are one decision
Jittered reconnects no storm after a restart

Fix layer: connection hold time in the application, then pool sizing across the fleet.

followUps.question: "Raise max_connections to 2,000."
followUps.html:
More concurrent work on the same cores makes every query slower.

Effect
Memory each connection reserves some
CPU more context switching and lock contention
Result the limit moves; the latency gets worse

followUps.question: 🧪 Autoscaling goes from 10 to 40 instances, each with a pool of 25.  is 500. What happens?
followUps.html:
The fleet can now ask for 1,000; the database refuses beyond 500.

10 × 25 = 250   ← fine
40 × 25 = 1,000 > 500
safe pool per instance at 40 instances: (500 − reserved) / 40 ≈ 12

followUps.question: What does "idle in transaction" tell you?
followUps.html:
The application started a transaction and went away.

  • It holds a connection and possibly locks, doing nothing.
  • Typical causes: a remote call inside the transaction, a missing commit on an error path, a forgotten console session.

followUps.question: You can't even connect to investigate. Now what?
followUps.html:
Use the reserved slots, then free some.

Steps:connect as a superuser on a reserved connectiongroup sessions by state and sourceterminate idle-in-transaction sessionsfind the cause

followUps.question: Why does a downstream slowdown show up as a database connection problem?
followUps.html:
Because requests hold their connection while they wait for something else.

Chain:a payment API slowsrequests hold a transaction open across the callconnections aren't returnedthe pool emptiesevery endpoint fails, including ones that never call payments

dontSay: "Raise the limit." — look at the sessions first.
"Bigger pools." — times how many instances?
"It's a database capacity problem." — often it's the application holding connections.
"We restarted and it went away." — it'll be back at the next peak.

databases-q43.testing: that you read the deadlock report, find the lock order the release changed, and fix the order instead of hiding the errors.
databases-q43.trap: adding a blanket retry and calling it solved.
databases-q43.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "A deadlock is two transactions each holding a lock the other needs. A spike right after a release means the release changed which locks are taken, or in what order, or for how long."
2 · Rule out the fakes "First I check they are deadlocks, and not lock-wait timeouts or serialisation failures, which look similar in an error dashboard and have different fixes. And whether traffic simply went up."
3 · Confirm with evidence "Then I read the database's deadlock report. It names both transactions, the statements they were running and the locks they held and wanted. I match those statements to the diff of the release."
4 · Fix by experiment "Usually it's one of four: a new code path locks the same rows in a different order; a bulk update without an order by; a foreign key or an update that lost its index; or a transaction that got longer. I fix that cause, starting with a consistent lock order."
5 · Validate "I reproduce it with a concurrent test running both paths, and confirm the rate goes back to baseline."
6 · Productionise "And I keep the retry, because a few deadlocks are normal, but alert on the rate and document the lock order."
Close "Read the report, find the changed order, fix the order; retries are the safety net."

stages.name: Name it
stages.html:
"Three properties of locking a deploy can alter."

Changed Example
Which rows are locked a new feature updates accounts inside the order transaction
The order the new path locks inventory then orders; the old one locks orders then inventory
How long a remote call or extra queries were added inside the transaction
How many a dropped index turns a row lock into a scan that locks many rows

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.html:
"Three errors that share a dashboard panel."

Error Meaning Fix direction
Deadlock detected (PostgreSQL 40P01, MySQL 1213) a cycle; one victim aborted lock ordering
Lock wait timeout (55P03, MySQL 1205) a queue behind a slow holder shorten the holder
Serialisation failure (40001) an isolation conflict retry; reduce contention
Other fake Check
More traffic, same rate per request deadlocks per thousand transactions, before and after
A batch job that happened to start then which sessions are in the reports
A migration running during the deploy schema-change locks in the report

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.claim: the deadlock report against the diff
stages.html:
"The report gives both sides." An illustrative PostgreSQL log entry:

ERROR: deadlock detected
DETAIL: Process 101 waits for ShareLock on transaction 5001; blocked by process 202.
        Process 202 waits for ShareLock on transaction 5002; blocked by process 101.
        Process 101: UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 'A1'
        Process 202: UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = 77
Read from the report Then
The two statements find each in the code; which is new or moved in this release?
The tables and rows the pair of resources locked in opposite orders
Whether both sides are the same statement a bulk update colliding with itself: unordered rows or gap locks

Rebuilt as a timeline, the report above is:

Time New path (process 101) Existing path (process 202)
1 updates order 77 updates inventory A1
2 updates inventory A1 updates order 77
cycle → one is aborted

On MySQL the equivalent is the latest-deadlock section of SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS, or all of them with innodb_print_all_deadlocks.

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.html:
"Four usual causes."

Experiment How Why Best suited when
E1 · One lock order both paths touch orders before inventory; rows by ascending id no cycle can form two code paths, opposite order
E2 · Order the bulk statement sort the ids; lock them up front with SELECT … ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE concurrent batches no longer cross the same statement on both sides
E3 · Restore the index index the foreign key or the WHERE column of the update fewer rows, and fewer gaps, are locked the release changed a query or dropped an index
E4 · Shorten the transaction move remote calls and unrelated work outside locks overlap for less time the transaction grew
Meanwhile roll back the release, or feature-flag the new path off stops the bleeding while the fix is built the rate is hurting users

stages.name: Validate
stages.html:
"A deadlock that can't be reproduced isn't known to be fixed."

Check Before After
A concurrent test: both paths in parallel on the same rows, many iterations deadlocks occur 0
Deadlocks per thousand transactions in production measure back to the pre-release baseline
Retries per request measure measure
Transaction duration, p99 measure measure

stages.name: Productionise
stages.claim: a documented order and a watched rate
stages.html:
"Deadlocks never reach zero; the rate must stay boring."

Practice Detail
A written lock order "parent before child; rows by ascending primary key" in the data-access guidelines
Retry on the deadlock error the whole transaction, with backoff and a cap
An alert on the rate, not the count per thousand transactions
All deadlock reports logged the evidence is there next time
Concurrency tests for write paths that share tables caught before release
Review of new transactions which tables, in what order, for how long

Fix layer: transaction design in the application; indexes so locks stay narrow.

followUps.question: "Wrap everything in a retry and move on."
followUps.html:
Retries hide the errors and keep the wasted work.

Retry only Fix the order
Errors seen by users fewer fewer
Work thrown away and redone still there, growing with load gone
At higher traffic retries collide again fine

followUps.question: 🧪 In the report above, which lock order would stop the cycle?
followUps.html:
Either one, as long as both paths use it.

both: orders first, then inventory
101: lock order 77 ✅ → lock A1 ✅ → commit
202: lock order 77 ⏳ → after 101 commits: ✅ → lock A1 ✅
wait-for graph: 202 → 101 only        ← a queue, no cycle

followUps.question: Both sides of the deadlock are the same UPDATE. How?
followUps.html:
Two runs lock overlapping rows in different orders.

  • UPDATE … WHERE id IN (…) has no guaranteed row order.
  • On InnoDB, gap locks on an indexed range can also cross.
  • Fix: process rows in key order, in smaller batches.

followUps.question: How can dropping an index cause deadlocks?
followUps.html:
Without it, the statement scans and locks far more than the rows it changes.

With the index Without
Locks the matching rows scans the table or a wide range, taking locks as it goes (engine-dependent)
Small chance of overlap large

followUps.question: How do you catch this before the next release?
followUps.html:
Test the write paths against each other.

Guard Catches
Concurrency tests that pair write paths sharing tables opposite lock orders
A canary with deadlock-rate comparison a spike on 5% of traffic
A review question: "which locks, in which order?" most of them, cheaply

dontSay: "Add retries." — as the fix.
"Raise the lock timeout." — a deadlock isn't a timeout.
"Lower the isolation level." — not without reading the report.
"It's just more traffic." — check the rate per transaction.

databases-q44.testing: that a delete marks rows dead and doesn't return space to the disk, and that something (often a long transaction) is stopping cleanup.
databases-q44.trap: running VACUUM FULL on a live table in the middle of the day.
databases-q44.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "This is bloat. In an MVCC database a delete doesn't remove the row; it marks that version dead. Cleanup later makes the space reusable inside the file, and usually doesn't give it back to the operating system."
2 · Rule out the fakes "First I check that the table is really shrinking in rows. Maybe inserts outpace deletes, or the growth is in the indexes or in large-value storage, or the deletes are soft deletes that only set a flag."
3 · Confirm with evidence "Then I look at dead rows against live rows, when cleanup last ran on that table, and what the oldest open transaction is. A transaction that's been open for hours stops vacuum from removing anything newer than its snapshot."
4 · Fix by experiment "So I end the long transaction or the stale replication slot first. Then I make autovacuum more aggressive for that table. To actually shrink the file, I rebuild online with a tool like pg-repack, or better, partition by time so old data is dropped, not deleted."
5 · Validate "I watch the dead-row count fall and the file size stop growing."
6 · Productionise "And I alert on transaction age and bloat, so cleanup never silently falls behind."
Close "Deletes create dead rows; find what's blocking cleanup; drop partitions where you can."

stages.name: Name it
stages.html:
"Three states of the space a deleted row used."

Lifecycle:live row ─DELETEdead version (still on the page)free space inside the filereturned to the disk

Shown on SQLite, where the free list plays the same role (run):

Step Pages in the file Free pages Rows
Load 20,000 rows 1,058 0 20,000
Delete 90% of them 1,058 924 2,000
Insert 5,000 more 1,058 661 7,000
VACUUM (a full rebuild) 371 0 7,000

The file didn't shrink after the delete. The free pages were reused by the next inserts, and only a rebuild made the file smaller.

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.html:
"Other reasons a table grows while 'deleting'."

Fake Check
Inserts outpace deletes row count over time
Soft deletes (deleted_at is set; nothing is removed) does the job run DELETE or UPDATE?
The growth is in the indexes table size against index size
Large values stored out of line (TOAST in PostgreSQL) size of the side storage
Heavy updates, not deletes every update also leaves a dead version
The delete job is failing or deleting nothing rows affected per run

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.claim: dead rows, last cleanup, oldest snapshot
stages.html:
"Three numbers." PostgreSQL names shown; other engines have equivalents.

Evidence Where Reading
Dead against live rows pg_stat_user_tables (n_dead_tup, n_live_tup) a large dead share → cleanup is behind
Last vacuum / autovacuum the same view long ago, on a busy table → it isn't triggering or finishing
The oldest open transaction pg_stat_activity (xact_start) hours old → it's pinning dead rows
Replication slots pg_replication_slots an inactive slot can hold cleanup back
Prepared (two-phase) transactions pg_prepared_xacts a forgotten one pins rows indefinitely
What blocks cleanup Why
A long-running transaction or an idle-in-transaction session its snapshot might still need the dead rows
A lagging replica with feedback enabled, or a stale slot the primary keeps rows the replica may need
Autovacuum thresholds too lazy for a huge table the default triggers on a percentage of the table
Autovacuum throttled or cancelled by locks it never completes a pass

On InnoDB the same problem appears as a growing undo history list while a long transaction is open, and as space that stays allocated to the table file after deletes.

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.html:
"In this order; the last step is optional."

Experiment How Why Best suited when
E1 · Remove the blocker end the long transaction; drop or repair the stale slot nothing else works until cleanup is allowed to proceed an old snapshot exists
E2 · Tune autovacuum for the table a lower scale factor and a higher cost limit on that table cleanup keeps pace with churn a large, busy table
E3 · Rebuild online pg_repack; REINDEX CONCURRENTLY for indexes returns space to the disk without a long lock the file must actually shrink
E4 · Partition by time delete becomes DROP PARTITION no dead rows are created at all retention-based deletes
Don't Because
VACUUM FULL on a live table it takes an exclusive lock for the whole rewrite
Disable autovacuum to "reduce load" it guarantees the bloat

stages.name: Validate
stages.html:
"What 'fixed' looks like."

Check Before After
Dead rows on the table measure falling after each vacuum
Table and index size over a week growing flat
Age of the oldest transaction hours seconds to minutes
Query latency on the table measure measure: fewer dead rows to skip

Flat is the goal. Space freed by an ordinary vacuum is reused; the file shrinks only after a rebuild.

stages.name: Productionise
stages.claim: cleanup that can't fall behind unseen
stages.html:
"Alert on the causes."

Practice Detail
Alert on transaction age and idle-in-transaction sessions the usual blocker
An idle-in-transaction timeout forgotten sessions end themselves
Bloat and dead-row ratio per table on a dashboard cleanup lag is visible
Per-table autovacuum settings for hot tables not the global default
Time-partition anything with a retention rule dropping replaces deleting
Monitor replication slots an abandoned one is a slow leak

Fix layer: transaction length in the application; cleanup settings and partitioning in the database.

followUps.question: "Run VACUUM FULL to get the space back."
followUps.html:
It rewrites the table under an exclusive lock.

VACUUM VACUUM FULL pg_repack
Blocks reads and writes no yes, for the whole rewrite only briefly
Returns space to the disk rarely yes yes

followUps.question: 🧪 In the SQLite run, how many pages does the file have right after deleting 90% of the rows?
followUps.html:
The same 1,058.

before delete: 1,058 pages, 0 free
after delete:  1,058 pages, 924 free      ← reusable, still in the file
after VACUUM:    371 pages                ← only the rebuild shrank it; run above

followUps.question: Why does one long transaction stop cleanup for the whole table?
followUps.html:
Its snapshot might still need any version that died after it started.

Rule:a row diesany snapshot older than that still open?keep itremovable

So a report left open since morning pins every row deleted since morning.

followUps.question: Do indexes bloat too?
followUps.html:
Yes, and they're cleaned differently.

  • Dead index entries are removed by vacuum; pages left sparse aren't merged back well.
  • Fix: REINDEX CONCURRENTLY, or the online rebuild.

followUps.question: How would you design a table that must drop 90 days of data every day?
followUps.html:
So that old data leaves by metadata, not by delete.

Design Daily removal
Daily or weekly partitions by time DROP (or detach) the oldest partition: instant, no dead rows
One big table with DELETE millions of dead rows, vacuum load, bloat

dontSay: "DELETE frees the space." — it marks rows dead.
"VACUUM FULL." — an exclusive lock on a live table.
"Turn autovacuum off, it's using I/O." — that causes the problem.
"The disk is full, add disk." — find the blocker.

databases-q45.testing: that you won't run one giant DELETE, and know the three shapes: drop a partition, batch by key, or copy-and-swap.
databases-q45.trap: DELETE FROM events WHERE created_at < … as a single statement.
databases-q45.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "First I ask what share of the table this is, whether the table is partitioned, whether it's a one-off or a recurring retention job, and what references these rows."
2 · Constraints and numbers "The limits are the same as for any change to a live table: no long locks, replicas must keep up, and no single transaction big enough to bloat the log or stall cleanup."
3 · Baseline design "If the table is partitioned by time, I drop the old partitions: that's a metadata operation. If it isn't, I delete in small batches by primary-key range, committing each batch and pausing when replica lag rises."
4 · Deep-dive "Each batch selects a few thousand ids in key order and deletes those. It's resumable and idempotent. And if I'm deleting most of the table, I do the opposite: copy the rows I'm keeping into a new table and swap."
5 · Failure modes "What goes wrong: cascades multiplying the work, an unindexed filter that scans the table for every batch, dead rows piling up faster than vacuum removes them, and CDC consumers getting two hundred million delete events."
6 · Evolve "Afterwards I partition the table by time, so the next retention run is a drop."
Close "Drop if you can, batch if you must, copy-and-swap when most of it goes."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
"Four answers pick the method."

Question Why it matters
What share of the table is being deleted? 10% → batch; 90% → copy the rest and swap
Is the table partitioned by the delete criterion? then it's DROP PARTITION
One-off or every night? recurring → fix the design, not only this run
Foreign keys, cascades, triggers? each deleted row may fan out
Must the rows be archived first? export, verify, then delete
Who consumes changes? (replicas, CDC, search) they receive every delete

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
"Why not a single DELETE."

One statement over 200 million rows Effect
One transaction locks held, and log retained, until it finishes
A failure at 95% rolls all of it back
Replicas replay it as one block: lag for its whole duration
Dead rows 200 million at once; cleanup can't start until commit 
rows            = 200,000,000
batch           = 5,000
batches         = 200,000,000 / 5,000      = 40,000
time per batch  = 0.3 s (work + pause)     ← illustrative
total           = 40,000 × 0.3 s           = 12,000 s ≈ 3.3 hours

A job of hours, so it has to be resumable and throttled.

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
"Choose by how the data is laid out and how much goes."

Method Lock Dead rows Log volume
Drop partition brief, metadata none tiny
Batched delete row locks per batch yes, cleaned as you go high, spread out
Copy and swap brief at the swap none in the new table the kept rows only
TRUNCATE exclusive none tiny; only when everything goes

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
"Small, ordered, committed batches." Run on SQLite through Python: 10 old rows and 3 current ones, batches of 4.

import sqlite3
d = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
d.execute("CREATE TABLE ev(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, created TEXT)")
d.executemany("INSERT INTO ev(created) VALUES (?)",
    [("2024-01-01" if i < 10 else "2026-10-01",) for i in range(13)])
batches = 0
while True:
    n = d.execute(
        "DELETE FROM ev WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM ev "
        "WHERE created < '2025-01-01' ORDER BY id LIMIT 4)").rowcount
    d.commit()                              # one short transaction
    if n == 0: break
    batches += 1                            # here: sleep if replicas lag
print(batches, "batches;",
      d.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ev").fetchone()[0], "rows kept")
# → 3 batches; 3 rows kept
Property How
Indexed filter an index on the delete criterion, or walk the primary key: otherwise each batch rescans
Resumable it stops when a batch deletes nothing; a restart just continues
Throttled pause on replica lag, lock waits or dead-row growth
Off-peak, but safe at any time each batch is small enough not to matter
Archive first, if required export the batch, verify, then delete it
Copy and swap:create the new tablecopy the rows to keep, in batchescapture changes made meanwhilebrief lockrenamedrop the old table

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
"Each side effect, and its guard."

Failure Cause Guard
Each batch is slow no index on the filter; the subquery scans index it, or iterate by primary-key range
The work multiplies ON DELETE CASCADE to child tables; triggers delete children first, in their own batches; an index on every child foreign key
The table doesn't shrink deletes leave dead rows expected; vacuum, or an online rebuild afterwards
Replicas lag the delete rate exceeds apply rate throttle on lag
CDC, search, caches flooded 200 million delete events warn the owners; filter or pause
Cleanup can't keep up a long transaction elsewhere pins the dead rows check transaction age first
The wrong rows a bad predicate dry-run a COUNT; a backup or archive before starting

Measure during the run: rows deleted per minute, replica lag, lock waits, dead rows, write latency on the table.

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
"Make the next one a metadata change."

Practice Detail
Partition by time retention = drop the oldest partition, on a schedule
A TTL feature where the store has one DynamoDB, Cassandra, MongoDB TTL indexes
A retention policy per table written down; a job, an owner, an alert if it stops
Archive tier old partitions exported to cheap storage before the drop

Fix layer: data lifecycle: partitioning in the schema, a batch job until then.

followUps.question: "DELETE FROM events WHERE created_at < '2025-01-01'; in one go, at night."
followUps.html:
One transaction for hours, whatever the hour.

One statement Batches
A failure near the end rolls back everything loses one batch
Replica lag for the whole run bounded per batch
Can be paused no yes

followUps.question: 🧪 200 million rows, 5,000 per batch. How many batches, and if each takes 0.3 s including the pause, how long?
followUps.html:
40,000 batches; about 3.3 hours.

200,000,000 / 5,000 = 40,000 batches
40,000 × 0.3 s      = 12,000 s ≈ 3.3 h

followUps.question: Why does the disk not free up afterwards?
followUps.html:
The rows are dead, not gone; the space is reusable inside the file.

After the delete:vacuumspace reused by new rowsreturned to the disk

See table-keeps-growing.

followUps.question: When is copy-and-swap better than deleting?
followUps.html:
When you're keeping the minority.

Deleting Better
10% of the table batched delete
90% of the table copy the 10%, swap: less work, no bloat, a compact table

followUps.question: The rows are referenced by three child tables with cascades. Plan?
followUps.html:
Delete bottom-up, explicitly.

Order:index every child foreign keydelete grandchildren in batcheschildrenparentsnever rely on the cascade for volume

A cascade turns one parent batch into an unbounded child delete inside the same transaction.

dontSay: "One DELETE, at night." — still one huge transaction.
"TRUNCATE." — that removes everything.
"The table will shrink." — not without a rebuild.
"Cascades will take care of the children." — in the same transaction, unbatched.

databases-q46.testing: that you can turn the two numbers into a backup design, and that "we have backups" means "we have restored them".
databases-q46.trap: calling a replica a backup, or quoting an RTO nobody has ever timed.
databases-q46.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "RPO is the recovery point objective: how much data, measured in time, we can afford to lose. RTO is the recovery time objective: how long we can afford to be down. Both come from the business."
2 · Mechanism "RPO is set by how often the data leaves the machine. A nightly backup means up to a day lost. Continuous log archiving brings it to seconds or minutes, and gives point-in-time recovery: restore the last base backup, then replay the log to a chosen moment. RTO is set by how long a restore takes, or by having a standby to fail over to."
3 · Where it breaks "It breaks in three ways. A replica isn't a backup: a bad delete replicates in milliseconds. A backup nobody has restored may be corrupt or incomplete. And the restore may take ten hours when the RTO says one."
4 · How I'd use it "So I schedule restores. Automatically, into a scratch environment, with checks on the result and a stopwatch. The measured time is the real RTO."
5 · Adjacent concept "High availability handles a node failing. Backups handle the data being wrong. You need both."
Close "RPO is how much you lose, RTO is how long you're down, and a backup counts only after a timed restore."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html:
"One looks back from the failure; the other looks forward."

        last recoverable point            failure                 service restored
───────────────┼─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┼──────────▶ time
               │◀──────── RPO ──────────────▶│◀────────── RTO ─────────▶│
                     data that is lost                 time down
RPO RTO
Question how much data can we lose? how long can we be down?
Unit time's worth of writes time
Set by how often data is copied off the machine how fast a restore or failover is
Smaller costs more frequent or continuous copying standbys, automation, rehearsal

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
"Each method, and the two numbers it produces."

Method RPO RTO Protects against
Nightly full backup up to 24 hours restore time for the whole database hardware loss, mistakes (to last night)
Base backup + continuous log archive (PITR) seconds to minutes restore + log replay mistakes: restore to just before them
Asynchronous replica the replication lag a failover: seconds to minutes node failure only
Synchronous replica zero a failover node failure only
Storage snapshots the snapshot interval fast to attach hardware; some mistakes
Logical dump when it ran slow for large data version upgrades, single-table restores
Point-in-time recovery:restore the latest base backupreplay the archived logstop just before the bad statementopen the database
restore time ≈ size ÷ restore throughput + log replay
500 GB ÷ 200 MB/s ≈ 2,500 s ≈ 42 min, plus replay           ← illustrative throughput

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
"Why 'we have backups' is often untrue."

Belief Reality
"The replica is our backup" DROP TABLE reaches the replica in milliseconds
"The backup job is green" the job ran; nobody knows the file restores
"Our RTO is one hour" measured by whom, on what data size?
"Backups are in the same account and region" the event that takes out the database takes them too
"We back up the database" and the encryption keys, roles, extensions, configuration?
Failure found only at restore Example
A gap in the log archive recovery stops hours short
A corrupt or truncated file the restore fails
A missing key or credential the encrypted backup can't be read
Restore slower than assumed the RTO was a wish
Ransomware reached the backups no immutable copy

stages.name: How I'd use it
stages.claim: a restore on a schedule, with a stopwatch
stages.html:
"A backup is proved by restoring it."

Drill:pick a backuprestore into an isolated environmentreplay the log to a target timerun checksrecord the durationtear down
Check after the restore Proves
The database starts and accepts queries the files are usable
Row counts and checksums against production at that time the data is complete
An application smoke test against it it's usable, not only readable
Elapsed time, end to end the real RTO
Latest recoverable timestamp the real RPO
Practice Detail
Automated, at least weekly an untested backup is unknown
3-2-1 three copies, two kinds of storage, one off-site
An immutable copy object lock or a separate account
A written runbook, and people who have run it restores happen at the worst moment
Alert on backup age and archive lag a silent failure shows within hours

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
"Two different failures, two different tools."

Failure Handled by
A node, disk or zone dies replicas and failover (HA)
The data is wrong: a bad deploy, a mistaken DELETE, corruption backups and point-in-time recovery
A region is lost cross-region replicas or backups (DR)
An attacker encrypts everything immutable, offline backups
Tier RPO / RTO a business might set Design
Payments, orders near zero / minutes synchronous replica + PITR
Core product data minutes / under an hour async replica + PITR
Analytics, logs hours / a day periodic snapshots

The tiers are illustrative; the real numbers are a business decision per dataset.

Fix layer: operations: backup design from the two numbers, proved by restore drills.

followUps.question: "We have three replicas, so we don't need backups."
followUps.html:
Replicas copy every change, including the wrong ones.

Event Replicas Backup + PITR
A node dies fail over slow
DELETE without a WHERE deleted everywhere restore to just before

followUps.question: 🧪 Full backup at 02:00, no log archiving. A bad migration corrupts data at 17:00. What's the best you can recover, and what's lost?
followUps.html:
The 02:00 state. Fifteen hours of writes are lost.

17:00 − 02:00 = 15 hours of data            ← the actual RPO, whatever the policy says
with continuous log archiving: replay to 16:59 → about a minute lost

followUps.question: Who decides the RPO and RTO?
followUps.html:
The business, per dataset, with the cost in front of them.

  • Engineering prices each option.
  • The business picks what an hour of downtime or lost data is worth.

followUps.question: How do you recover one table that was dropped an hour ago?
followUps.html:
Restore elsewhere to just before the drop, then copy the table back.

Steps:PITR into a scratch instance, to one minute beforeexport the tableimport into productionreconcile writes made since

followUps.question: How do you protect backups from ransomware or a compromised admin?
followUps.html:
Make at least one copy impossible to change from production.

Control Effect
Immutable storage (object lock, WORM) can't be deleted or encrypted during retention
A separate account with separate credentials production access doesn't reach it
Delete protection and delayed deletion time to notice
Restore drills from that copy proves the isolated copy works

dontSay: "Replicas are our backup." — they replicate mistakes.
"The backup job succeeded." — has it been restored?
"Our RTO is an hour." — timed when?
"RPO zero, RTO zero." — at what cost, and does the business need it?

databases-q48.testing: that you choose the key from the queries, check for skew, and have a plan for the tenant that outgrows a shard.
databases-q48.trap: sharding on an auto-increment id or a timestamp, or sharding before a single node is exhausted.
databases-q48.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "First I ask whether we need to shard yet. Indexes, replicas, partitioning and a bigger node come first. Then I ask for the queries, because the key is chosen from them."
2 · Constraints and numbers "A good key does three things: most queries touch one shard, load spreads evenly, and the key never changes for a row. I'd want the tenant size distribution, because one giant tenant changes the answer."
3 · Baseline design "In a multi-tenant product nearly every query is scoped to a tenant, so tenant id is the key. Every table carries it, and a tenant's joins and transactions stay on one shard."
4 · Deep-dive "The weakness is skew. So I don't hash tenants straight to shards. I use a directory that maps each tenant to a shard, which lets me give a large tenant its own shard and move tenants without rehashing everyone."
5 · Failure modes "What still hurts: cross-tenant reports, which fan out to every shard; globally unique ids; and a tenant too big for one node, which needs a second-level key inside it."
6 · Evolve "I'd watch load per shard and per tenant, and rebalance by moving tenants online."
Close "Tenant id through a directory: local queries, and a way out for the outliers."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: do we need shards, and what are the queries
stages.html:
"Sharding is the last step, so I check the earlier ones."

Before sharding:indexes and query fixesread replicascachingpartitioninga larger node ─measured write or size limitshard
Access pattern Scope Needs a transaction?
A tenant's users, projects, invoices one tenant yes, within the tenant
A tenant's dashboard joins one tenant no
Login by email global no
Admin report across all tenants all tenants no

Three of four are scoped to one tenant. That decides the key.

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
"Each candidate against the three tests."

Candidate key Queries stay on one shard Load is even Never changes
tenant_id yes, for tenant-scoped work only if tenants are similar in size yes
Row id (hash) no: a tenant is spread over every shard yes yes
Auto-increment id (range) no no: all new writes hit the last shard yes
created_at (range) no no: "now" is one hot shard yes
region partly no: a few values can change

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
"The key is in every table and every query."

projects(tenant_id, id, name, …)   PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, id)
invoices(tenant_id, id, …)         PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, id)
Design rule Reason
tenant_id leads every primary key and index routing and seeking use the same prefix
Every query carries tenant_id the router sends it to one shard
Joins and transactions stay inside a tenant they stay on one shard
Small global tables (plans, countries) copied to every shard as reference tables
Login by email a small global lookup: email → tenant

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.claim: skew, and the directory that absorbs it
stages.html:
"One large tenant makes one hot shard." Simulation: 39 tenants of 100 rows and one of 6,000, hashed to 4 shards.

import hashlib
def shard(key, n=4):
    return int(hashlib.md5(str(key).encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % n
tenants = {f"t{i}": 100 for i in range(1, 40)}
tenants["big"] = 6000                       # one giant tenant
by_tenant, by_row = [0] * 4, [0] * 4
for t, rows in tenants.items():
    by_tenant[shard(t)] += rows
    for r in range(rows):
        by_row[shard(f"{t}:{r}")] += 1
print(by_tenant)
print(by_row)
# → [6900, 1100, 1100, 800]
# → [2434, 2490, 2513, 2463]

Hashing by row is even and useless: every tenant query now hits all four shards.

The fix keeps the key and changes the mapping:

Mapping Placement Moving a tenant
hash(tenant_id) % N fixed by arithmetic changing N remaps almost everyone
A directory: tenant_id → shard chosen per tenant; the giant gets its own shard copy the tenant, flip one directory row

The directory is small, read on every request and rarely written, so it is cached and replicated.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
"Each loss needs an answer before launch."

Loss Answer
Cross-tenant queries fan out and merge, or run them on a warehouse fed by CDC
Cross-shard transactions designed out; where unavoidable, a saga
Global uniqueness (email, ids) a global lookup table; ids that embed the shard or are UUIDs
A tenant too large for one node a second-level key inside that tenant (tenant_id, project_id)
The directory is down cached in the router; it is the most available component
Schema changes run on every shard; versions must tolerate being mixed

Measure: rows, queries per second and storage per shard and per tenant; the share of queries that touch more than one shard.

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
"Growth is handled by moving entries in the directory."

Move a tenant:copy to the new shardreplicate changes until caught upbrief write pause for that tenantflip the directory rowdelete the old copy
Stage Change
Today tenants packed onto a few shards by the directory
A tenant grows moved to its own shard, online
Regulation the directory also places a tenant in a region
Many small tenants packed densely; noisy ones are rate-limited per tenant

Fix layer: data model (the key on every table) and routing (the directory).

followUps.question: "Shard on the primary key so load is perfectly even."
followUps.html:
Even load, and every useful query becomes a scatter.

Key One tenant's dashboard
Row id asks every shard, merges the results
tenant_id asks one shard

followUps.question: 🧪 Four shards by ; you add a fifth. Roughly what share of tenants move?
followUps.html:
About four in five.

a tenant stays only if  h % 4 == h % 5
that holds for 4 residues out of every 20   ← h % 20 in {0, 1, 2, 3}
stay = 4 / 20 = 20%      move = 80%

Consistent hashing or a directory moves only what has to move.

followUps.question: How do you run a report across all tenants?
followUps.html:
Not on the shards.

  • Occasional: fan out to every shard and merge.
  • Regular: a warehouse fed by CDC from all shards.

followUps.question: How do you generate unique ids across shards?
followUps.html:
Ids that can't collide by construction.

Scheme Note
(tenant_id, local id) composite key simplest; unique within the tenant
A time-ordered id with a shard or node part sortable, no coordination
Random UUID unique; poor index locality

followUps.question: When would you choose a database per tenant?
followUps.html:
When isolation matters more than operating cost.

Model Pick when
Shared tables, tenant_id column many small tenants; lowest cost
A schema or database per tenant strict isolation, per-tenant backup and restore, few large tenants
A mix through the directory most products: small tenants shared, large ones dedicated

dontSay: "We'll shard" as the first fix for a slow database. — replicas and partitioning first.
"Hash the primary key." — every tenant query fans out.
"Shard by date." — today is one hot shard.
"Tenants are about the same size." — measure the distribution.

databases-q49.testing: that you name the dual-write problem, reach for the transactional outbox, and say that consumers must be idempotent.
databases-q49.trap: "commit, then publish" (or the reverse) with a retry, as if that made it atomic.
databases-q49.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "This is the dual-write problem. A database commit and a broker publish are two systems, so they can't be one atomic step. First I ask what's worse here: a lost event, or a duplicate."
2 · Constraints and numbers "Usually a lost event is unacceptable and a duplicate is tolerable. So I want at-least-once delivery, and a bound on how late an event may be."
3 · Baseline design "I use a transactional outbox. In the same local transaction that inserts the order, I insert a row into an outbox table. Both commit or neither does."
4 · Deep-dive "A relay then reads the outbox and publishes: a poller, or change data capture on the log. It marks a row as sent only after the broker acknowledges."
5 · Failure modes "If the relay crashes after publishing and before marking, the event goes out twice. So every event carries an id, and the consumer records ids it has processed and skips repeats."
6 · Evolve "For a flow across several services I chain these into a saga, with a compensating action per step."
Close "One local transaction, at-least-once delivery, idempotent consumers."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
"Either order of two writes has a gap."

Order Crash in the gap Result
Commit, then publish after the commit an order exists and nobody is told
Publish, then commit after the publish an event announces an order that doesn't exist
Publish inside the transaction the commit fails after the publish the same phantom event

A retry narrows the gap. It doesn't close it: the process can die before it retries.

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
"Three delivery guarantees; one is practical."

Guarantee Meaning Cost
At-most-once may lose an event none; unacceptable for orders
At-least-once never loses; may repeat consumers must be idempotent
Exactly-once effect at-least-once delivery + an idempotent consumer a processed-ids record
Number to agree Why
Maximum delay from commit to publish sets the polling interval or justifies CDC
Ordering needed? per order, or global decides the partition key
How long consumers remember ids bounds the dedupe table

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.claim: the outbox row in the same transaction
stages.html:
"The event becomes data in my own database first."

outbox(id, aggregate_id, topic, payload, created_at, sent_at)

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.claim: atomic write, duplicate delivery, one effect
stages.html:
"A crash before commit leaves nothing; a duplicate is absorbed." Run on SQLite through Python.

import sqlite3
o = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
o.executescript("CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, total INT);"
                "CREATE TABLE outbox(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, payload TEXT,"
                " sent INT DEFAULT 0);")
def place_order(total, crash=False):
    try:
        with o:                                # one local transaction
            oid = o.execute("INSERT INTO orders(total) VALUES (?)",
                            (total,)).lastrowid
            o.execute("INSERT INTO outbox(payload) VALUES (?)", (str(oid),))
            if crash: raise RuntimeError("crash before commit")
    except RuntimeError: pass
place_order(50); place_order(70, crash=True)
print(o.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders").fetchone()[0], "orders,",
      o.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM outbox").fetchone()[0], "outbox rows")
seen, delivered = set(), []
for mid, payload in o.execute("SELECT id, payload FROM outbox").fetchall():
    for _ in range(2):                         # the relay publishes twice
        if mid not in seen: seen.add(mid); delivered.append(payload)
print("delivered:", delivered)
# → 1 orders, 1 outbox rows
# → delivered: ['1']
Relay style How Pick when
Polling select unsent rows every interval; mark sent after the ack simple; a delay of the interval is fine
CDC on the log a log reader streams outbox inserts to the broker low delay; no polling load

Ordering: publish with the aggregate id (the order id) as the partition key, so one order's events stay in order.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
"Every crash point ends in a retry or a duplicate, never a loss."

Crash point State left Outcome
Before the commit no order, no outbox row nothing happened
After the commit, before the publish an unsent row the relay publishes it later
After the publish, before "mark sent" still unsent published again → the consumer dedupes
The broker is down rows accumulate published when it returns; alert on backlog
The consumer fails mid-way no ack redelivered; its work and its "processed" record commit together
Also watch Guard
The outbox table grows delete or archive sent rows
A poison event blocks the queue a dead-letter queue after N attempts
Several relays SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, or a single leader

Measure: outbox backlog and the age of the oldest unsent row.

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
"One outbox per service, chained."

Saga:order placedpayment takenstock reservedcompensate: refund paymentcancel order
Option Atomic across systems? Why I do or don't
Outbox no: eventual, never lost the default
Saga no: each step is local, with a compensation multi-service business flows
Two-phase commit yes blocks if the coordinator fails; few brokers support it
Event sourcing the event log is the write when the events are the model, not a side effect

Fix layer: write path in the service; idempotency in every consumer.

followUps.question: "Publish after the commit, and retry on failure."
followUps.html:
The process can die between the commit and the publish, and the retry dies with it.

Gap:commit crashpublish never runsnothing records that an event is owed

The outbox row is that record.

followUps.question: 🧪 The relay publishes event 17, then crashes before marking it sent. What does the consumer see?
followUps.html:
Event 17 twice. Its effect is applied once.

relay restarts → row 17 still unsent → publishes 17 again
consumer: 17 already in processed_events → skip          ← at-least-once + idempotent

followUps.question: How does a consumer become idempotent?
followUps.html:
It makes "already done" a fact it can check.

Technique How
A processed-events table insert the event id in the same transaction as the work; a unique-key violation means skip
A naturally idempotent write "set status = paid", not "add 1"

followUps.question: Polling or CDC for the relay?
followUps.html:
Polling to start; CDC when delay or load matters.

  • Polling: nothing new to run; adds query load and a delay.
  • CDC: near-real-time and in commit order; one more system to operate.

followUps.question: Why not two-phase commit?
followUps.html:
It trades availability for atomicity, and most stacks can't run it.

Two-phase commit Outbox
If the coordinator fails participants hold locks and wait nothing is blocked
Broker support rare any broker
Consistency atomic eventual, with no loss

dontSay: "I'd wrap both in a transaction." — the broker isn't in the database's transaction.
"Commit, then publish, with retries." — the crash is between them.
"The broker gives exactly-once." — the effect is exactly-once only with an idempotent consumer.
"Duplicates won't happen." — they're the price of never losing an event.

databases-q55.testing: that the hard part is semantics, not syntax, and that safety includes "plausible wrong numbers", not just dropped tables.
databases-q55.trap: "the model generates SQL against our warehouse schema", read-write, with no semantic layer.
databases-q55.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask which metrics executives actually ask about, which warehouse, who owns the definitions, and what the data-access rules are."
2 · Constraints and numbers "The constraints are cost and trust. A bad join over a large fact table can scan a huge amount of data, so every query has a time limit and a scan limit. And a wrong number in a board deck is worse than an error."
3 · Baseline design "Generating valid SQL is the easy part. The hard part is meaning: what 'revenue' is here, which date defines 'last quarter', which of three customer tables is the real one. So the agent queries a curated semantic layer, with governed metric definitions and approved views, not raw tables. For common metrics it calls metric tools and writes no SQL at all."
4 · Deep-dive "Then verification. It shows the SQL and the definitions it used, checks results against known totals or the previous period, and when a question is ambiguous it asks, or states its assumption."
5 · Failure modes "The failures that matter are plausible wrong answers: a wrong definition, a join that double-counts, stale data. Safety is read-only credentials scoped to the user, row-level security in the database, and select statements only."
6 · Evolve "It grows by adding metrics and views where unanswered questions cluster, with a golden set of business questions checked by result."
Close "The risk isn't a dropped table; it's a confident number that's wrong."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: users, questions, data and its owners
stages.html:
"Four questions, and the third is the one teams skip."

Question Sets
Which metrics do executives ask about? the metric tools to build first
Which warehouse, how large? cost limits
Who owns each definition? the semantic layer's governance
What may each user see? row-level security

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
"Every query runs inside limits set before the model writes anything."

per-question budget (illustrative)
at most 3 model steps: understand, query, explain
per query: time-out 30 s · scan cap · row cap 10,000
answer in under about 10 s for a metric tool; longer for ad-hoc SQL, with progress shown
Limit Prevents
Time-out and scan cap a runaway query bill
Row cap a result too large for the context

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
"The agent's choices are narrowed to correct ones."

Path:questionambiguous? askmetric tool if one fitsSQL over approved viewslimits + read-onlysanity checkanswer with SQL and definitions
Control Setting Prevents
Credentials read-only role, user-scoped, row-level security writes; data leaks
Statements SELECT only, by a parser allow-list schema or data changes
Scope approved views and metric definitions wrong tables and definitions
Limits time-out, scan cap, row cap runaway cost
Output SQL + definitions + assumptions shown silent wrong numbers
Check compare with known totals or the prior period implausible results

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
"A query that runs cleanly proves nothing about meaning."

Ambiguous term Possible readings What the agent does
"Revenue" gross, net of refunds, recognised uses the governed metric; names it
"Last quarter" calendar, fiscal; order date or invoice date asks, or states the assumption
"Customers" accounts, users, paying accounts asks, or states the assumption
Verify:resultcompare with a trusted dashboard totalflag, don't present

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
"None of these raises an error."

Failure Control
A wrong metric definition metric tools from the semantic layer
A fan-out join double-counts documented joins; sanity checks on totals
Stale data data freshness shown with the answer
Instructions hidden in data values read-only, no actions; results are treated as data
Different SQL on each run metric tools make the common answers deterministic

stages.name: Evolve
stages.claim: grow the semantic layer from questions
stages.html:
"Unanswered questions are the roadmap."

Loop:log unanswered or corrected questionscluster themadd metrics and viewsadd golden cases
Golden question Expected result Runs
"Net revenue last fiscal quarter" the governed total measure, several times
An ambiguous question a clarifying question or a stated assumption measure

Evaluation hook: golden business questions compared by result set, not by SQL text. Fix layer: retrieval/data (the semantic layer) and permission system.

followUps.question: Why not give it the whole schema?
followUps.html:
Hundreds of tables overwhelm the context and invite wrong joins.

Whole schema Curated layer
Many plausible, wrong choices fewer, correct ones
Definitions chosen by the model definitions governed by owners

followUps.question: "Read-only means it's safe."
followUps.html:
It stops damage to the data, and nothing else.

  • Not prevented: a wrong number in a board deck.
  • Not prevented: a full table scan with a large bill.

followUps.question: 🧪 Two runs give different revenue numbers for the same question. Why?
followUps.html:
Different SQL each time, so a different definition each time.

run 1: SUM(order_total)                    ← gross
run 2: SUM(order_total) − SUM(refunds)     ← net
fix: a governed "net_revenue" metric tool, so the definition isn't chosen per run

followUps.question: How do you evaluate it?
followUps.html:
Golden business questions with known results.

  • Compared by result set, not by SQL text.
  • Run several times for consistency.
  • Including ambiguous questions, where the right behaviour is to ask.

dontSay: "We give the model the schema and run whatever it writes." — no semantic layer, no limits.
Safety that's only about DROP TABLE. — the costly failure is a wrong number.
"The query ran, so the answer is right." — running isn't meaning.
